function makeMermaidImage(svg) { const img = document.createElement("img"); const doc = parser.parseFromString(svg, "image/svg+xml"); const svgEl = doc.querySelector("svg"); const { maxWidth } = svgEl?.style || {}; const firstTitle = doc.querySelector("title"); const firstDesc = doc.querySelector("desc");
img.setAttribute("src", `data:image/svg+xml,${encodeURIComponent(svg)}`); if (maxWidth) { img.width = parseInt(maxWidth); } if (firstTitle) { img.setAttribute("alt", firstTitle.textContent); } if (firstDesc) { const caption = document.createElement("figcaption"); caption.className = "sr-only"; caption.textContent = firstDesc.textContent; return [img, caption]; } return [img]; }
async function makeMermaidError(text) { let errorMessage = ""; try { await mermaid.parse(text); } catch (err) { errorMessage = `${err}`; }
const result = document.createElement("details"); result.className = 'jp-RenderedMermaid-Details'; const summary = document.createElement("summary"); summary.className = 'jp-RenderedMermaid-Summary'; const pre = document.createElement("pre"); const code = document.createElement("code"); code.innerText = text; pre.appendChild(code); summary.appendChild(pre); result.appendChild(summary);
const warning = document.createElement("pre"); warning.innerText = errorMessage; result.appendChild(warning); return [result]; }
async function renderOneMarmaid(src) { const id = `jp-mermaid-${_nextMermaidId++}`; const parent = src.parentNode; let raw = src.textContent.trim(); const el = document.createElement("div"); el.style.visibility = "hidden"; document.body.appendChild(el); let results = null; let output = null; try { const { svg } = await mermaid.render(id, raw, el); results = makeMermaidImage(svg); output = document.createElement("figure"); results.map(output.appendChild, output); } catch (err) { parent.classList.add("jp-mod-warning"); results = await makeMermaidError(raw); output = results[0]; } finally { el.remove(); } parent.classList.add("jp-RenderedMermaid"); parent.appendChild(output); }

<main> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=57c86778-33e8-4388-aeb7-b4465b70ae37"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <h1 id="The-Fokker-Planck-Equation-and-Diffusion-Models">The Fokker Planck Equation and Diffusion Models<a class="anchor-link" href="#The-Fokker-Planck-Equation-and-Diffusion-Models">¶</a></h1> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=cbc53980-3790-4983-b83d-0d32bea01df4"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>In this tutorial, we continue our ride into the theory of diffusion models and stochastic differential equations (SDEs). We are going to derive the <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fokker%E2%80%93Planck_equation">Fokker-Planck equation</a>, one of the fundamental equations of stochastic analysis that expresses SDEs as partial differential equations (PDEs). This equation then allows us to describe our backward sampling process in diffusion models as an ordinary differential equation (ODE). <strong>In other words, we can sample from diffusion models by only sampling noise once at the start and iteratively applying a deterministic function.</strong> Such a sampling process is now widely used in generative models such as <a href="https://stability.ai/">stable diffusion</a>.</p> <p>More specifically, we are going to learn:</p> <ol> <li><strong>What it is:</strong> What the Fokker-Planck equation actually says.</li> <li><strong>Intuition:</strong> What the Fokker-Planck equation describes intuitively. This involves understanding the concept of divergence.</li> <li><strong>Ito's Lemma:</strong> The fundamental building block for deriving the Fokker-Planck equation.</li> <li><strong>Derivation:</strong> The actual derivation of the Fokker-Planck equation.</li> <li><strong>Application to diffusion models</strong> We show how this theory can applied to diffusion models to enable the ODE formulation of diffusion models.</li> </ol> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=1b24363d-5fdb-4018-a0e0-35cbc455a5fb"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p><strong>Prerequisites.</strong> This tutorial is part of a <a href="https://www.peterholderrieth.com/blog/">tutorial series</a> on diffusion models. We recommend reading the blogpost about <a href="https://www.peterholderrieth.com/blog/2023/Diffusion-Models-with-Stochastic-Differential-Equations-A-Introduction-with-Self-Contained-Mathematical-Proofs/">diffusion models with SDEs</a> before this tutorial.</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=e9efa6cd-1059-4c69-91a1-a37fcfb50dd6"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <h2 id="1.-What-is-the-Fokker-Planck-Equation?">1. What is the Fokker-Planck Equation?<a class="anchor-link" href="#1.-What-is-the-Fokker-Planck-Equation?">¶</a></h2> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=be9bf68f-3721-41be-a0a7-2c7354aa66e4"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p><strong>Setting.</strong> Let's consider the Ito stochastic differential equation (Ito-SDE) with drift coefficients $f:\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^d$ and diffusion coefficients $g:\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$: $$\begin{align*} dX_t = f(X_t,t)dt + g(X_t,t)dW_t \end{align*}$$ and some start distribution $X_0\sim \mu$. Let's define the distribution $p_t(x)$ to be the distribution of $X_t$, i.e. $X_t\sim p_t$. In other words, there is a probability flow $p:\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ changing over time. Let's write $p_t(x) = p(x,t)$.</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=ee6a2926-6168-4961-a5c4-417bca6257c5"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p><strong>Focker Planck Equation.</strong> The Focker Planck equation describes how the distribution $p_t$ changes over time. <strong>The significance of the Focker Planck equation is that the change of a probability density over time can solely be expressed as derivatives over coordinates $x$:</strong></p> <p>$$ \begin{align*} \frac{d}{dt}p_t(x) =& -\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\left[f_i(x,t)p_t(x)\right] + \frac{1}{2}\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}\sum\limits_{j=1}^{n}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x_i\partial x_j}\left[[g(x,t)g(x,t)^T]_{ij}p_t(x)\right]\\ =& -\nabla\cdot [fp_t]+\frac{1}{2}[\nabla^2\cdot [gg^Tp_t]]\\ \end{align*} $$</p> <p>where we use the notation $\nabla \cdot$ (resp. $\nabla^2\cdot$) to describe the sum of all pairwise partial derivatives (resp. second partial derivatives) of the corresponding components. In physics, one also calls $\nabla \cdot [fp_t]$ the <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divergence">divergence</a> of $fp_t$.</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=b30388d0-b884-4123-aa43-7773b7033ed4"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <h2 id="2.-Let's-intuitively-understand-the-equation">2. Let's intuitively understand the equation<a class="anchor-link" href="#2.-Let's-intuitively-understand-the-equation">¶</a></h2> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=a5041298-79d4-47c8-89b8-6356ff349675"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>In this chapter, we are going to derive an intuitive understanding of the Fokker Planck formula. As we will see later, one can find a technical proof for it but I think there is a lot of value in understanding what the formula actually says intuitively. It basically boils down to understanding the divergence $\nabla\cdot$ and the <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuity_equation">continuity equation</a> of an incompressible flow. We go through both concepts step-by-step.</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=fcfa7609-b728-4c7e-8bd8-3fe07c392069"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>Let us look at the Fokker Planck equation again. The equation describes how an infinitesimal probability, i.e. a density $p_t(x)$, changes over time. The change can be described by the net inflow of a probability. If probability mass moves to $x$, then $\frac{d}{dt}p_t(x)>0$. If it moves away from $x$, then $\frac{d}{dt}p_t(x)<0$. In essence, we know that $$ \begin{align*} \frac{d}{dt}p_t(x) = \text{"Net inflow of change of probability mass to point }x\text{"} \end{align*} $$ However, what is that net inflow? In physics, this is called <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divergence">divergence</a>. And we are going to explain in the next chapter how that concept is derived. If you are already very familiar with divergence, this section can safely be skipped.</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=95aef06c-ebec-46cd-b2a2-f6dcb895fb6f"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <h3 id="2.1.-A-derivation-of-the-divergence-formula">2.1. A derivation of the divergence formula<a class="anchor-link" href="#2.1.-A-derivation-of-the-divergence-formula">¶</a></h3> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=81417e63-2596-4d6c-a0b3-cfa60b5ef1e9"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>Before we get to deep into SDEs, let's first understand divergence in a simpler setting. Let's assume that we are given a vector field $F:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d$. Let's try to describe the infinitesimal flux around $x_0$. When we say "infinitesimal", we mean "in the limit". We define it in the limit because it is not clear apriori how to define the flux in and out of a single point $x_0$. However, we have an intuitive idea of the flux in and out of a ball around an $\epsilon$-ball $B(x_0,\epsilon)$ around $x_0$. We can describe it by the formula: $$ \begin{align*} \text{Flux}_{\epsilon}(F)(x)=\frac{1}{\text{Vol}(B(x_0,\epsilon))}\int\limits_{\partial B(x_0,\epsilon)}F^T(x)\frac{x-x_0}{\|x-x_0\|}dS(x) \end{align*} $$ where the terms in the formula are:</p> <ol> <li><p><strong>Volumn:</strong> $\text{Vol}(B(x_0,\epsilon))$ is the volumn (i.e. Lebesgue-integral) of the epsilon-ball around $x_0$. We normalize by the volume.</p> </li> <li><p><strong>Boundary:</strong> $\partial B(x_0,\epsilon)$ is the boundary (i.e. the surface) of the epsilon-ball. We only integrate over the boundary of the epsilon ball because that's where something can flow in or out.</p> </li> <li><p><strong>Normal vector:</strong> the vector $x$ describe a point on the surface and $\frac{x-x_0}{\|x-x_0\|}$ is the normalized unit vector from pointing from $x_0$ to $x$.</p> </li> <li><p><strong>Vector flow</strong>: the value $F(x)$ gives the flow at $x$. However, not all of the "flow" points inwards and outwards of the epsilon-ball. Therefore, we decompose the value of $F(x)$ by: $$\begin{align*} F(x) =:& \left(F(x)-F(x)^T\frac{x-x_0}{\|x-x_0\|}\frac{x-x_0}{\|x-x_0\|}\right)+F(x)^T\frac{x-x_0}{\|x-x_0\|}\frac{x-x_0}{\|x-x_0\|}\\ =:&v_{\perp}+v_{\parallel} \end{align*}$$ for vectors $v_{\perp}$ and $v_{\parallel}$. We know that $v_{\perp}$ is tangential to the surface of $B(x_0,\epsilon)$ ball because it is orthogonal to the normal - this can be seen by computing $(x-x_0)^Tv_{\perp}=0$. Therefore, the direction $v_{\perp}$ has a net influx/outflow of zero. Therefore, the flux is simply given by the vector $v_{\perp}$ that points in the direction of the normal with length $$\begin{align*} F(x)^T\frac{x-x_0}{\|x-x_0\|} \end{align*}$$ Note that the length has a sign, it is negative if the perpendicular flow points inwards.</p> </li> <li><p><strong>Integral</strong>: Finally, we take the integral over all these flow values to get the total value of the inward/outward flow. We write $dS(x)$ to describe the surface integral over the surface $\partial B(x_0,\epsilon)$. If you are not yet comfortable with surface integrals, it actually does not really matter. Our proofs works without having ever computed a surface integral and you can simple think of it as a integral over a uniform space over the surface.</p> </li> </ol> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=e34c11be-da0f-476b-bd7a-a55ded3f5624"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=ef6c4a86-3825-4ae4-ba9f-dea243115e89"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p><strong>Divergence-Infinitesimal outflux.</strong> Let's rewrite the $\epsilon$-Flux around $x_0$ by setting $x-x_0=w$ for a unit vector $w$ and center the function flow:</p> <p>$$ \begin{align*} \text{Flux}_{\epsilon}(F)(x)=&\frac{1}{\text{Vol}(B(x_0,\epsilon))}\int\limits_{\partial B(x_0,\epsilon)}F^T(x)\frac{x-x_0}{\|x-x_0\|}dS(x)\\ =&\frac{1}{\text{Vol}(B(0,\epsilon))}\int\limits_{\partial B(0,\epsilon)}F^T(x_0+w)\frac{w}{\|w\|}dS(w) \end{align*} $$</p> <p>Next, let's use the following properties for volumes and surface areas: $$\begin{align*} \text{Vol}(B(0,\epsilon))&=\epsilon^{d}\text{Vol}(B(0,1))\\ \text{S}(\partial B(0,\epsilon))&=\epsilon^{d-1}\text{S}(\partial B(0,1)) \end{align*}$$ and simply the equation further $$ \begin{align*} \text{Flux}_{\epsilon}(f)(x) =&\frac{1}{\text{Vol}(B(0,\epsilon))}\int\limits_{\partial B(0,\epsilon)}F^T(x_0+w)\frac{w}{\|w\|}dS(w)\\ =&\frac{1}{\epsilon^{d}\text{Vol}(B(0,1))}\epsilon^{d-1}\int\limits_{\partial B(0,1)}F^T(x_0+\epsilon z)zdS(z)\\ =&\frac{1}{\epsilon\text{Vol}(B(0,1))}\int\limits_{\partial B(0,1)}F^T(x_0+\epsilon z)zdS(z) \end{align*} $$</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=4d945ac8-dd6e-4cfa-b790-b28b842a759f"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>Let's use a first-order Taylor approximation to get: $$F(x_0+\epsilon z) \approx F(x_0) + \epsilon DF(x_0)z$$ And therefore,</p> <p>$$ \begin{align*} F(x_0+\epsilon z)^Tz \approx& F^T(x_0)z + [\epsilon DF(x_0)z]^Tz\\ =& F^T(x_0)z + \epsilon z^TDF(x_0)z\\ =& \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}F_i(x_0)z_i + \epsilon\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}\sum\limits_{j=1}^{n}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}F_j(x_0)z_iz_j \end{align*}$$</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=7353363c-7daa-4bb7-a991-2a6267988c4b"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>Finally, let's substitute that in the integral equation of the flux to get: $$\begin{align*} \text{Flux}_{\epsilon}(F)(x) =&\frac{1}{\epsilon\text{Vol}(B(0,1))}\int\limits_{\partial B(0,1)}F^T(x_0+\epsilon z)zdS(z)\\ \approx &\frac{1}{\epsilon\text{Vol}(B(0,1))}\int\limits_{\partial B(0,1)} \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}F_i(x_0)z_i + \epsilon\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}\sum\limits_{j=1}^{n}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}F_j(x_0)z_iz_jdS(z)\\ =&\frac{1}{\epsilon\text{Vol}(B(0,1))}\left[\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}F_i(x_0)\int\limits_{\partial B(0,1)} z_idS(z) + \epsilon\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}\sum\limits_{j=1}^{n}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}F_j(x_0)\int\limits_{\partial B(0,1)}z_iz_jdS(z)\right] \end{align*} $$</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=cf868fc5-4d41-4d86-9787-3c9afd108fac"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>Now, it is obvious that $$\begin{align*} &\int\limits_{\partial B(0,1)}z_idS(z) = 0 \end{align*}$$ as the average of a component is zero as a sphere is symmetric. In addition, we derive for an arbitrary $j$ $$ \begin{align*} S(\partial B(0,1))=&\int\limits_{\partial B(0,1)}1 dS(z)=\int\limits_{\partial B(0,1)}\sum\limits_{i=1}^{d}z_i^2dS(z)=\sum\limits_{i=1}^{d}\int\limits_{\partial B(0,1)}z_i^2dS(z)=d\int\limits_{\partial B(0,1)}z_j^2dS(z)\\ \end{align*} $$ where we used the symmetry of the sphere. Therefore, $$\begin{align*} \int\limits_{\partial B(0,1)}z_j^2dS(z) = \frac{1}{d}S(\partial B(0,1)). \end{align*}$$</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=2c30fd3b-4204-4600-b63a-667692ce23f7"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>For $i\neq j$, let $A$ be the function $A(z)=z_iz_j$ and $R$ the rotation matrix defined by: $$ \begin{align*} R_{kl} = \begin{cases} -1 &\text{for }k=i,l=j\\ 1 &\text{for }k=j,l=i\\ 1&\text{for }k=l, k\neq i,j\\ 0&\text{for }k\neq l, (k,l)\neq (i,j), (k,l)\neq (j,i)\\ \end{cases} \end{align*} $$ Then $A(R(z))=(-z_j)z_i=-A(z)$ and therefore, by a change of variable $$ \begin{align*} \int z_iz_jdS(z) &= \int A(z) dS(z) = \int A(Rz)dS(z) = \int (-z_j)z_idS(z) = -\int z_jz_idS(z) \end{align*} $$ which implies that $$ \begin{align*} &0=2\int z_jz_idS(z) \Rightarrow 0=\int z_jz_idS(z). \end{align*} $$ for $i\neq j$.</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=c435d705-4f16-470e-985a-0c137dd7718b"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>With that, we get the final formula: $$\begin{align*} \text{Flux}_{\epsilon}(F)(x) =&\frac{1}{\epsilon\text{Vol}(B(0,1))}\left[\frac{\epsilon S(\partial B(0,1))}{d}\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}F_i(x_0)\right]+o(\epsilon)\\ =&\frac{1}{\text{Vol}(B(0,1))}\left[\frac{S(\partial B(0,1))}{d}\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}F_i(x_0)\right]+o(\epsilon)\\ \end{align*} $$</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=103e49ec-c6c2-4198-8d73-8591696733a5"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>Therefore, the flux is given by: $$\begin{align*} \text{div}(F)(x_0) = \lim\limits_{\epsilon\to 0}\text{Flux}_{\epsilon}(F)(x_0) =\frac{S(\partial B(0,1))}{d\text{Vol}(B(0,1))}\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}F_i(x_0) \end{align*}$$</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=8f189b16-69c9-48c7-9447-35c7f5c66094"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p><strong>Getting rid of constant factors.</strong> Finally, we use the formula for the volume and surface area of the epsilon ball: $$\begin{align*} S(\partial B(0,1)) &= \frac{2\pi^{d/2}}{\Gamma(\frac{d}{2})}\\ \text{Vol}(B(0,1)) &= \frac{2\pi^{d/2}}{\Gamma(\frac{d}{2}+1))} \end{align*} $$ and the use the property of the gamma function $\Gamma(x+1)=x\Gamma(x)$ to get: $$\begin{align*} \frac{S(\partial B(0,1))}{d\text{Vol}(B(0,1))} =&\frac{\frac{2\pi^{d/2}}{\Gamma(\frac{d}{2})}}{d\frac{2\pi^{d/2}}{\Gamma(\frac{d}{2}+1))}} =&\frac{\Gamma(\frac{d}{2}+1)}{d\Gamma(\frac{d}{2})} = 1 \end{align*} $$ By plugging this into the above equation we finally get the desired formula.</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=ba2b960e-136e-425c-9aa4-aa6e69a8e64d"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p><strong>Summary.</strong> In sum, we have derived that our physically intuitive net outwards flow is given by the divergence defined as: $$\text{div}(F)(x_0) = \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i} F_i(x_0)=[\nabla\cdot F](x_0)$$</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=da48c75d-0a5e-48a4-9328-46781d082d22"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <h3 id="2.2.-The-Fokker-Planck-Equation-as-a-Continuity-Equation">2.2. The Fokker-Planck Equation as a Continuity Equation<a class="anchor-link" href="#2.2.-The-Fokker-Planck-Equation-as-a-Continuity-Equation">¶</a></h3> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=454b230c-fa55-47bb-8bc7-190bba3b9f9f"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>Let us revisit our intuitive derivation of the Fokker-Planck equation applying what we just learnt about divergence: $$ \begin{align*} \frac{d}{dt}p_t(x)=&\text{"Net inflow of change of probability mass to point }x\text{"}\\ =&-\text{"Net outflow of change of probability mass to point }x\text{"}\\ =& -\text{div}(\text{"Change of probability mass at point }x\text{"})\\ =& -\nabla\cdot(\text{"Change of probability mass at point }x\text{"}) \end{align*} $$</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=eff2765d-e231-4212-969e-e96de16ecff3"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>In fact, we can also rewrite the Fokker-Planck equation in such a form as: $$ \begin{align*} \frac{d}{dt}p_t(x) =& -\nabla\cdot [fp_t+\frac{1}{2}\nabla^T[gg^Tp_t]]\\ \end{align*} $$</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=36285a51-6336-4a41-8583-0b371bcaab6c"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>An equation in such a form is usually called a <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuity_equation">continuity equation</a> on an incompressible fluid - incompressible means here simply that the probability cannot vanish but can also change its distribution throughout the space. We can see the two summands of $fp_t+\frac{1}{2}\nabla^Tgg^Tp_t$ have a very intuitive explanation:</p> <ol> <li><strong>Drift component</strong>: the vector field $f(x,t)$ pushes $x$ into the direction of $f(x,t)$. However, $f(x,t)$ cannot be the changed of probability for the following reason: if $p_t(x)=0$, then the change is also zero - as there was no probability mass at $x$ in the first place. We should weigh it by $p_t(x)$ to account for that, i.e. $f(x,t)p_t(x)$ is the vector field describing the change of probability given by the deterministic drift. In other words, $$ \begin{align*} \text{"Change of probability mass at point }x\text{ by drift $f$"} = f(x,t)p_t(x). \end{align*}$$</li> <li><strong>Diffusion component</strong>: the diffusion matrix $g(x,t)$ takes a small vector $\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}_d)$ and adds a small bit of noise $\sqrt{s}g(x,t)\xi \sim\mathcal{N}(0,sg(x,t)g(x,t)^T)$ where $s$ is a small step size. Therefore, the probability mass that is dispersed at point $x$ is proportional to the initial mass $p_t(x)$ and the rate of dispersion $g(x,t)g(x,t)^T$, i.e. $$\begin{align*} \text{"Dispersion of probability mass at }x\text{"} \propto p_t(x)g(x,t)g(x,t)^T \end{align*} $$ However, dispersion in itself does not change the probability mass as all neighboring points of $x$ also disperse probability mass with the approximately same rate. Therefore, we need to use the <strong>change of dispersion rate</strong>, i.e. this is described by the term: $$ \begin{align*} \text{"Change of probability mass }x\text{ by diffusion $g$"} = \frac{1}{2}\nabla[g(x,t)g^T(x,t)p_t(x)] \end{align*}$$ I acknowledge this is not a rigorous derivation (especially, where does the factor $\frac{1}{2}$ come from?) - but rather an intuitive explanation for the formula. We are going to derive it in the next chapter rigorously (e.g. you will see that the factor $\frac{1}{2}$ comes from the 2nd-order Taylor approximation).</li> </ol> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=192aba37-56ab-4f9a-92d2-fea80574a044"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p><strong>In essence, the Fokker-Planck equation describes the change of probability mass at $x$ over time as the net inflow of change of probability mass at $x$ given by a vector field describing the change of probability mass given by the SDE equation.</strong></p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=5d68a31e-13da-44b6-8115-6f85bb50beb2"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p><strong>Note:</strong> this nice interpretation of the Fokker-Planck equation came out of a <a href="https://mathoverflow.net/questions/461035/interpretation-of-second-order-term-in-fokker-planck-equation">discussion on stack overflow</a>.</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=940b04ed-9a2d-4532-9403-e374f18ea3e3"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <h2 id="3.-Ito's-Lemma">3. Ito's Lemma<a class="anchor-link" href="#3.-Ito's-Lemma">¶</a></h2> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=ae91c2a1-1474-4092-b6ae-8062948d92b4"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>In this chapter, we are going to derive <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It%C3%B4%27s_lemma">Ito's Lemma</a>. This is a fundamental building block in the theory of stochastic differential equations and is going to be a fundamental building block to derive the Fokker-Planck equation.</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=7648f223-8104-470e-8fe8-9902808f1bbd"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>Let $X_t$ the stochastic process defined by the SDE above. Out of such a stochastic process, one can construct a new stochastic process $Y_t=\eta(X_t)$ via an arbitrary smooth function $\eta:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$. A natural question that arises is: <strong>is the stochastic process $Y_t$ again described by an SDE and if yes, what are its drift and variation coefficients?</strong> The answer is yes, and Ito's Lemma describes the drift and variation coefficients of $Y_t$. Namely, Ito's lemma says that:</p> <p>$$\begin{align*} dY_t = \bar{f}(X_t,t)dt + \bar{g}(X_t,t)dt \end{align*} $$ where $$ \begin{align*} \bar{f}(x,t) &= \nabla\eta(x)^Tf(x,t)+\text{Tr}(g(x,t)^T\nabla^2\eta(x)g(x,t))\\ \bar{g}(x,t) &= \sqrt{\nabla\eta(x)^Tg(x,t)g(x,t)\nabla\eta(x)}\\ \end{align*} $$</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=3ab76a34-e4f8-49da-9cb7-ac02a57c30a3"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>Note that the above SDE is slightly different than the ones we have seen so far. The left-hand side defines $Y_t$ but the right-hand side also depends on $X_t$.</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=a25b02b7-7a00-4d52-8354-015f2958985c"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p><strong>Proof.</strong> We write $o(h^2)$ for an arbitrary function $g:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ such that $\lim\limits_{h\to 0}\frac{g(h)}{h^2}=0$. $$ \begin{align*} Y_{t+h} =& \eta(X_{t+h})\\ \approx& \eta(X_{t}+hf(X_t,t)+\sqrt{h}g(X_t,t)\epsilon)\\ =&\eta(X_t)+\nabla\eta(X_t)^T\left[hf(X_t,t)+\sqrt{h}g(X_t,t)\epsilon\right] +\frac{1}{2}\left[hf(X_t,t)+\sqrt{h}g(X_t,t)\epsilon\right]^T\nabla^2\eta(X_t)^T\left[hf(X_t,t)+\sqrt{h}g(X_t,t)\epsilon\right]+o(h^2)\\ =&Y_t+\nabla\eta(X_t)^T\left[hf(X_t,t)+\sqrt{h}g(X_t,t)\epsilon\right] +\frac{1}{2}h^2f(X_t,t)^T\nabla^2\eta(X_t)f(X_t,t)+\sqrt{h}h[g(X_t,t)\epsilon]^T\nabla^2\eta(X_t)f(X_t,t)+h\epsilon^Tg(X_t,t)^T\nabla^2\eta(X_t)g(X_t,t)\epsilon+o(h^2)\\ \end{align*}$$</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=0d02122b-02ba-43e0-a750-2e67e587d872"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>It holds that: $$ \begin{align*} \bar{f}(x,t) =&\lim\limits_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}\left(\mathbb{E}[Y_{t+h}-Y_t|X_t]\right)\\ =&\lim\limits_{h\to 0}\mathbb{E}\left[\nabla\eta(X_t)^T\left[f(X_t,t)+\frac{1}{\sqrt{h}}g(X_t,t)\epsilon\right] +\frac{1}{2}hf(X_t,t)^T\nabla^2\eta(X_t)f(X_t,t)+\sqrt{h}[g(X_t,t)\epsilon]^T\nabla^2\eta(X_t)f(X_t,t)+\epsilon^Tg^T(X_t,t)\nabla^2\eta(X_t)g(X_t,t)\epsilon|X_t\right]\\ =&\nabla\eta(X_t)^Tf(X_t,t)+\text{Tr}\left(g(X_t,t)^T\nabla^2\eta(X_t)g(X_t,t)\right)\\ \end{align*} $$ where we just used the fact that $\epsilon$ is independent of $X_t$ and that $\mathbb{E}[\epsilon^TA\epsilon]=\text{Tr}(A)$ for an arbitrary matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ and $\epsilon\sim\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$.</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=395b1bc8-290c-43d7-9ccc-b7fecfca65f8"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>Next, we get that: $$ \begin{align*} \bar{g}(x,t)^2=&\lim\limits_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}\mathbb{V}[Y_{t+h}-Y_t|X_t] \\ =&\lim\limits_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}\mathbb{V}\left[\nabla\eta(X_t)^T\sqrt{h}g(X_t,t)\epsilon +\sqrt{h}h[g(X_t,t)\epsilon]^T\nabla^2\eta(X_t)f(X_t,t)+h\epsilon^Tg(X_t,t)^T\nabla^2\eta(X_t)g(X_t,t)\epsilon\right|X_t]\\ =&\lim\limits_{h\to 0}\mathbb{V}\left[\nabla\eta(X_t)^Tg(X_t,t)\epsilon +h[g(X_t,t)\epsilon]^T\nabla^2\eta(X_t)f(X_t,t)+\sqrt{h}\epsilon^Tg(X_t,t)^T\nabla^2\eta(X_t)g(X_t,t)\epsilon\right|X_t]\\ =&\mathbb{V}\left[\nabla\eta(X_t)^Tg(X_t,t)\epsilon|X_t\right]\\ =&\nabla\eta(X_t)^Tg(X_t,t)[\nabla\eta(X_t)^Tg(X_t,t)]^T\\ =&\nabla\eta(X_t)^Tg(X_t,t)g(X_t,t)^T\nabla\eta(X_t)\\ \end{align*} $$</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=3e9e5827-3f74-464f-83f1-ce9d991e67f4"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>where we just the fact that $\mathbb{V}[A\epsilon]=\mathcal{N}(0,AA^T)$ for any matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{c\times d}$ and $\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{1}_d)$.</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=53496542-f60c-44bc-8cb1-645d0d4ad3f7"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <h2 id="4.-Deriving-the-Fokker-Planck-equation">4. Deriving the Fokker Planck equation<a class="anchor-link" href="#4.-Deriving-the-Fokker-Planck-equation">¶</a></h2> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=0a5dcdf9-fe6c-4b5c-a00c-41730fcc1d79"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>Next, let's start deriving the Fokker-Planck equation and let's fix a point $x_0\in\mathbb{R}^d$. Let's define $\eta_k(x) =\mathcal{N}(x;x_0,\frac{1}{k^2})$ to be the Gaussian kernel centered around $x_0$. Then we know that for an arbitrary smooth and regular function $F:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ it holds that: $$\begin{align} F(x_0) = \lim\limits_{k\to\infty}\int \eta_k(x)F(x)dx \end{align} $$ In particular, it holds that: $$\begin{align*} p_t(x_0) =& \lim\limits_{k\to\infty}\int \eta_k(x)p_{t}(x)dx\\ =&\lim\limits_{k\to\infty}\mathbb{E}[\eta_k(X_t)] \end{align*} $$</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=4c55f52e-3c24-4282-9860-8d2860db6997"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>By Ito's lemma, we know that $Y_t^{k}=\eta_k(X_t)$ follows the SDE $$\begin{align*} \frac{d}{dt}\mathbb{E}[\eta_{k}(X_t)]=& \mathbb{E}\left[\nabla\eta_k(X_t)^Tf(X_t,t)+\text{Tr}(g(t)^T\nabla^2\eta_k(X_t)g(t))\right] \end{align*} $$ (in expectation, one can remove the diffusion part of Ito's Lemma). This gives us:</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=7beec4a1-6594-4391-96e2-1565309539f4"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>$$ \begin{align*} &\frac{d}{dt}p_t(x_0)\\ =&\frac{d}{dt}\lim\limits_{k\to\infty}\mathbb{E}[\eta_k(X_t)]\\ =&\lim\limits_{k\to\infty}\frac{d}{dt}\mathbb{E}[\eta_k(X_t)]\\ =&\lim\limits_{k\to\infty}\mathbb{E}\left[\nabla\eta_k(X_t)^Tf(X_t,t)+\text{Tr}(g(X_t,t)^T\nabla^2\eta_k(X_t)g(X_t,t))\right]\\ =&\lim\limits_{k\to\infty}\int\left[\nabla\eta_k(x)^Tf(x,t)+\text{Tr}(g(X_t,t)^T\nabla^2\eta_k(x)g(X_t,t))\right]p_t(x)dx\\ =&\lim\limits_{k\to\infty}\left[\int\nabla\eta_k(x)^Tf(x,t)p_t(x)dx+\int\text{Tr}(g(X_t,t)^T\nabla^2\eta_k(x)g(X_t,t))p_t(x)dx\right]\\ =&\lim\limits_{k\to\infty}\left[-\int\eta_k(x)^T\nabla\cdot[f(x,t)p_t(x)]dx+\int\text{Tr}(g(X_t,t)^T\nabla^2\eta_k(x)g(X_t,t))p_t(x)dx\right]\quad\text{(using partial integration)}\\ =&-\nabla\cdot[f(x_0,t)p_t(x_0)]+\lim\limits_{k\to\infty}\int\text{Tr}(g(X_t,t)^T\nabla^2\eta_k(x)g(X_t,t))p_t(x)dx \end{align*}$$</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=8b9281e0-d814-48e8-8942-ed60e10f1f3a"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>Let's compute the second term: $$ \begin{align*} &\int\text{Tr}(g(x,t)^T\nabla^2\eta_k(x)g(x,t))p_t(x)dx\\ =&\sum\limits_{l=1}^{d} \int\left[g(t)^T\nabla^2\eta_k(x)g(t)\right]_{ll}p_t(x)dx\\ =&\sum\limits_{l=1}^{d} \int p_t(x)\sum\limits_{j=1}^{d}g_{jl}(t)[\nabla^2\eta_k(x)g(t)]_{jl}dx\\ =&\sum\limits_{l=1}^{d}\sum\limits_{j=1}^{d}\sum\limits_{i=1}^{d} \int \left[p_t(x)g_{jl}(t)g_{il}(t)\right]\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x_j\partial x_i}\eta_k(x)dx\\ =&\sum\limits_{l=1}^{d}\sum\limits_{j=1}^{d}\sum\limits_{i=1}^{d} \int \eta_k(x)\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x_j\partial x_i}\left[p_t(x)g_{jl}(t)g_{il}(t)\right]dx\quad\text{(using partial integration twice)}\\ \to& \sum\limits_{l=1}^{d}\sum\limits_{j=1}^{d}\sum\limits_{i=1}^{d} \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x_j\partial x_i}\left[p_t(x_0)g_{jl}(x_0,t)g_{il}(x_0,t)\right]\quad(\text{for }k\to\infty)\\ =& \sum\limits_{j=1}^{d}\sum\limits_{i=1}^{d} \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x_j\partial x_i}\left[p_t(x_0)[g(x_0,t)g^T(x_0,t)]_{ji}\right]\\ \end{align*} $$</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=5eb54839-925e-4dc8-89ca-9dbc082cf4fa"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>This finishes the proof for the Fokker-Planck equation. <strong>In essence, the Fokker-Planck equation can be derived by applying Ito's Lemma on a kernel function $\eta_k$ that enclose an $\epsilon$-ball around a point $x_0$ for $\epsilon\to 0$.</strong></p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=9d6e15f5-8e1d-45e6-9388-e4c73b183f4a"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <h2 id="5.-Expressing-SDEs-via-ODEs">5. Expressing SDEs via ODEs<a class="anchor-link" href="#5.-Expressing-SDEs-via-ODEs">¶</a></h2> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=3b259fbf-00d2-4540-94ae-f8b96d836aed"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>Next, we are applying the Fokker-Planck equation to show that the result of every SDE can be achieved by also running an ODE - if we had full information. Let us revisit the SDE given by:</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=e718b833-ab7c-4e03-beab-211e628bab6f"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>$$ \begin{align*} dX_t = f(X_t,t)dt + g(t)dW_t \end{align*}$$</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=e065a3fb-dd5a-4bfe-a9d0-54fba6cba44a"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>For simplicity, we made a small change and made $g$ independent of the location - which is always case in standard diffusion models and many other settings.</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=33285d64-1faf-4352-a6e9-1f2cb5cb8488"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>A natural question is to ask: <strong>Could achieve the same effect by also running an ODE instead of an SDE as long as we have the same initial distribution?</strong>. More specifically, if we started with an initial distribution $X_0\sim p_0$, would there be an ODE of the form $$ \begin{align*} dZ_t = F(Z_t,t)dt \end{align*}$$ for some $F:\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^d$ such that if $Z_0$ and $X_0$ have the same distribution, then also $Z_t$ and $X_t$ have the same distribution? The answer is yes and we are going to show why now.</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=3417b16c-ca84-4505-9778-e7db1614bd1e"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>Let $X_t\sim p_t$ and let's assume that $Z_0\sim p_0$. Then compute:</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=dce40cd7-3f90-4fe7-a106-b122a2c9cf69"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>$$ \begin{align*} \frac{d}{dt}p_t(x) =& -\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\left[f_i(x,t)p_t(x)\right] + \frac{1}{2}\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x_i\partial x_j}\left[[g(t)g(t)^T]_{ij}p_t(x)\right]\\ =& -\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\left[f_i(x,t)p_t(x)\right] + \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\sum\limits_{j=1}^{n}\frac{1}{2}\left[[g(t)g(t)^T]_{ij}\right]\frac{\partial}{\partial x_j}p_t(x)\quad\text{(derivatives are linear)}\\ =& -\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\left[f_i(x,t)p_t(x)\right] + \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\sum\limits_{j=1}^{n}\frac{1}{2}\left[[g(t)g(t)^T]_{ij}\right]\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial x_j}\log p_t(x)\right]p_t(x)\quad\text{(derivative of log)}\\ =& -\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\left[\left[f_i(x,t) -\frac{1}{2}\sum\limits_{j=1}^{n}\left[[g(t)g(t)^T]_{ij}\right]\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial x_j}\log p_t(x)\right]\right]p_t(x)\right] \quad\text{(derivatives are linear)}\\ =& -\nabla\cdot[Fp_t](x) \end{align*} $$ for $F$ defined by: $$ \begin{align*} F(x,t)= f(x,t)-\frac{1}{2}g(t)g(t)^T\nabla\log p_t(x)\quad\text{(SDE-2-ODE)} \end{align*} $$</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=99ff1c8b-e059-46e3-b8c1-518cf6f3aae1"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p><strong>In other words, we have shown that the effect of an SDE can be achieved by running an ODE. However, we would need to know the score function $\nabla\log p_t(x)$.</strong></p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=0b8e10dc-9421-4a8a-a4ab-ff7fedde6913"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <h2 id="6.-Application-to-diffusion-models">6. Application to diffusion models<a class="anchor-link" href="#6.-Application-to-diffusion-models">¶</a></h2> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=3a4f4da1-bcb2-4579-b88d-d71da8a86bd2"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>Finally, we combine everything together to change the sampling process of diffusion models. Sampling in diffusion models works by running the backwards SDE given by: In other words, the reverse-time SDE is given by: $$\begin{align*} d\bar{X}_t= [f(X_t,t)-g^2(t)\nabla\log p_{t}(\bar{X}_t)]dt + g(t)d\bar{W}_t \end{align*}$$ where time is running backwards in this case (see <a href="https://www.peterholderrieth.com/blog/2023/Diffusion-Models-with-Stochastic-Differential-Equations-A-Introduction-with-Self-Contained-Mathematical-Proofs/">this tutorial</a> for an explanation). The functions $f,g$ are user-defined and the score $\nabla\log p_{t}$ is learnt during training. To convert this SDE into an ODE with the same final distribution, we use the formula above (SDE-2-ODE) to get: $$ \begin{align*} d\bar{X}_t= [f(X_t,t)-\frac{1}{2}g^2(t)\nabla\log p_{t}(\bar{X}_t)]dt \end{align*} $$ where we added $\frac{1}{2}g^2(t)\nabla\log p_t(x)$ - instead of substracted - from the drift coefficients as we run time backwards.</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=604f6265-b6c5-4821-87d4-3b70acedcff1"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>We added the option to sample via this ODE formulation to our diffusion model codebase by simply not adding noise and only running the ODE with the drift coefficient above.</p> </div> </div> </div> </div><div class="jp-Cell jp-CodeCell jp-Notebook-cell jp-mod-noOutputs" id="cell-id=7b6732ef-16ab-4b86-9511-5ddf05132053"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p><strong>Introduction.</strong> In our <a href="https://www.peterholderrieth.com/blog/2023/Classifier-Guidance-For-Diffusion-Models/">previous tutorial</a>, we showed how we can build a <strong>conditional</strong> image generation machine. By training a classifier on noisy data, we could successfully turn an unconditional diffusion model into a conditional diffusion. Great!</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=fcbc8999-836f-42eb-84dc-e01266f1a261"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p><strong>What is the problem with what we have?</strong> However, there are a few problems with that approach. One is obvious and the other one is a bit more intricate:</p> <ol> <li><p><strong>Training an extra classifier:</strong> as we learnt, we need to train an extra classifier on noisy data. This takes approximately as much time as training the diffusion model itself, so we essentially double our work. We can't use an off-the-shelf classifier (e.g. an ImageNet classifier) either as we require it to be trained on noisy data.</p> </li> <li><p><strong>Adversarial generation:</strong> there is an interesting question to what extend classifier guidance actually generates a realistic image or only an image that the classifier considers to be most likely of a certain class. In a way, one might object that we essentially perform an adversarial attack on the image classifier (i.e. make it believe that the image is a certain class) rather than generating an actually realistic image.</p> </li> </ol> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=3e6621c7-ec5f-4c21-a1f7-02650c10a50f"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p><strong>Main idea.</strong> The main idea behind classifier-free guidance is that you <strong>train two diffusion models: 1) a conditional and 2) an unconditional generation model in one model at the same time</strong>. One can then balance the conditional and unconditional part to ensure that the images are highly realistic but also fulfill the desired condition.</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=2662e77e-646d-4861-9859-91f58445dddf"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>We again consider the task of sampling from the distribution $p(x|y)$ with diffusion models. Again, we would convert the data distribution $p_{0}(x|y)=p(x|y)$ into a noised distribution $p_{1}(x|y)$ gradually over time via an SDE with $X_t\sim p_{t}(x|y)$ for all $0\leq t \leq 1$. Again, we want an approximation of the score $\nabla_{x_t} \log p(x_t|y)$ for a conditional variable $y$. But first, let's do a quick reminder about our current scenario.</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=b0a67b13-cc54-4c7b-a6e1-44394be2c1f7"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <h2 id="1.-Reminder---diffusion-models-with-SDEs">1. Reminder - diffusion models with SDEs<a class="anchor-link" href="#1.-Reminder---diffusion-models-with-SDEs">¶</a></h2><p>We again assume that we are in the scenario where we run a forward and backward SDE as in our <a href="https://www.peterholderrieth.com/blog/2023/Diffusion-Models-with-Stochastic-Differential-Equations-A-Introduction-with-Self-Contained-Mathematical-Proofs/">previous tutorials</a>. In particular, there is a forward SDE: $$ \begin{align*} dX_t = f(X_t,t)dt + g(t)dW_t \end{align*} $$ with $X_0\sim p_{\text{data}}=p_0$ and $p_{1} \approx \mathcal{N}(0,\mathbb{V}[X_1])$ and the drift coefficients are affine, i.e. $f(x,t)=a(t)x+b(t)$. As we saw, it holds that we can compute closed analytical formulas for $m(x,t)=\mathbb{E}[X_t|X_0=x]$ and $\mathbb{V}[X_t|X_0]$ where $v(t) = \mathbb{V}[X_t|X_0]$ is independent of $X_t$ and $X_0$.</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=6e0bc842-c6e3-4cdc-bb5c-645a07139154"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>In our case, we use the <a href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/1503.03585.pdf">variance-preserving SDE</a> (see <a href="https://www.peterholderrieth.com/blog/2023/Diffusion-Models-with-Stochastic-Differential-Equations-A-Introduction-with-Self-Contained-Mathematical-Proofs/">here</a> for an explanation), where $$\begin{align*} f(x,t)&=-x\frac{\beta_{\text{min}}+t(\beta_{\text{max}}-\beta_{\text{min}})}{2}\\ g(t)&=\sqrt{\beta_{\text{min}}+t(\beta_{\text{max}}-\beta_{\text{min}})}\\ m(x,t)&=x\exp\left(-\frac{1}{4}t^2(\beta_{\text{max}}-\beta_{\text{min}})-\frac{1}{2}t\beta_{\text{min}}\right)\\ v(t)&=1-\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}t^2(\beta_{\text{max}}-\beta_{\text{min}})-t\beta_{\text{min}}\right) \end{align*}$$</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="2.-Classifier-free-network-architecture">2. Classifier-free network architecture<a class="anchor-link" href="#2.-Classifier-free-network-architecture">¶</a></h2><p><strong>Going from conditional generation to a classifier.</strong> Let's imagine that we had a conditional generative model $p(x_t|y)$ available. Then we could simply invert it to a classifier by: \begin{align*} p_t(y|x_t) = \frac{p_t(x_t|y)}{p_t(x_t)}p_t(y) \end{align*} And if we wanted to do classifier-guidance with this implicit classifier, we would compute the classifier gradient $c(x_t,t)$ by \begin{align*} c(x_t,t) = \nabla_{x_t} \log p_t(y|x_t) = \nabla_{x_t} \log p_t(x_t|y) - \nabla_{x_t} \log p_t(x_t) \end{align*} To sample from a conditional diffusion model, we would then run the reverse SDE with the combined score where we weight the classifier gradient with a weight $w\in\mathbb{R}$: \begin{align*} \nabla_{x_t}\log p_t(x_t|y) =& \nabla_{x_t} \log p_t(x_t|y) + w*c(x_t,t) \\ =& (1+w)\nabla_{x_t} \log p_t(x_t|y) - w*\nabla_{x_t} \log p_t(x_t) \end{align*} What is written above is very intuitive: we go into the direction of score of the conditional model. However we scale up that score with $s$, we need to substract the score of the unconditional model. <strong>In theory, there is no better or worse $s$. In fact, $w=0$ should give equally good results.</strong> However, in turns out that in practice (for some delicate reasons I will explain later), choosing $w$ is important to achieve high performance.</p> <p><strong>Training with classifier-free guidance.</strong> The idea of classifier-free guidance is to train two a conditional and an unconditional generative model in one model simultanously and use the above equation to get the conditional score. We simply introduce a special token $\varnothing$ indicating that we do not specify a class. Our variable $y$ then can take either be a class variable or $\varnothing$. More specificaly, our denoising neural network $\epsilon_{\theta}(x_t,t,y)$ is again a rescaled score network: $$\begin{align*} \epsilon_{\theta}(x_t,t,y) = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{v(t)}}s_{\theta}(x_t,t,y) \end{align*}$$ and takes three inputs:</p> <ol> <li>The noised image/data point $x_t$</li> <li>A time variable $t\in [0,1]$.</li> <li>A conditional variable $y$ which is either $\varnothing$ or a class variable.</li> </ol> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=5740d6d6-fbb3-4b99-a533-066712ef14f3"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" Classifier-Free Guidance Training<a class="anchor-link" href="#3.-Classifier-Free-Guidance-Training">¶</a></h2> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=f68acfc8-01cb-4659-920d-6ad746b8f341"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>As said above, our goal is to approximate $$\begin{align*} s_{\theta}(x_t,t,y) \approx \begin{cases} \nabla_{x_t}\log p(x_t)\quad\text{if } y=\varnothing\\ \nabla_{x_t}\log p(x_t|y)\quad\text{ if } y\neq\varnothing\\ \end{cases} \end{align*}$$ Our goal is to have one denoising model $\epsilon_{\theta}(x_t,t,y)=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{v(t)}}s_{\theta}(x_t,t,y)$ approximating it. We can train it by standard denoising score matching, i.e. by predicting the noise that perturbed our data point. In essence, we train both the conditional and the unconditional case at the same time.</p> <p>Therefore, it is natural to design our training algorithm works as follows:</p> <ol> <li>Sample $(x,y)\sim p_{\text{data}}(x,y)$ (i.e. randomly draw images and labels from our train data)</li> <li>With probability $p_{\text{uncond}}$, set $y=\varnothing$ (i.e. randomly discard labeling)</li> <li>Sample random noise $\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I})$</li> <li>Run SDE forward, i.e. set: $x_t =m(x,t) + \sqrt{v(t)}\epsilon$</li> <li>Compute loss: $$\begin{align*} L(\theta) = \|\epsilon_{\theta}(x_t,t,y)-\epsilon\|^2 \end{align*} $$</li> <li>Take gradient step on $\theta$ minimizing $L(\theta)$.</li> </ol> <p>Of course, we compute the above computation in mini batches of data.</p> </div> </div> </div> </div><div class="jp-Cell jp-CodeCell jp-Notebook-cell jp-mod-noOutputs" id="cell-id=00ef9ea5-d052-4a75-b415-bd8f6bfab8ff"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"> <div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt">In [8]:</div> <div Classifier-Free Guidance Sampling<a class="anchor-link" href="#4.-Classifier-Free-Guidance-Sampling">¶</a></h2><p>Finally, if we want to sample from our diffusion model, we execute the following algorithm:</p> <p>Given conditional variable $y$, a guidance weight $w$ and number of grid points $k$.</p> <ol> <li>Initialize: $x_{1}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}_{d})$.</li> <li>For $i=1,\dots,k$: sample $\epsilon_i\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{1})$ and perform a time-reversal step of the SDE with the classifer-free guidance score:</li> </ol> <p>$$ S = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{v(i/k)}}\left[(1+w)\epsilon_{\theta}(x_{i/k},i/k,y)-w \epsilon_{\theta}(x_{i/k},i/k,\varnothing)\right] $$ $$\begin{align*} x_{i/k} = x_{(i-1)/k} + \frac{g^2(i/k)S-f(x_{i/k},i/k)}{k} + g(i/k) \epsilon_i \end{align*}$$</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=a12e6539-73b8-421a-8265-a1a070c3f1db"> <div id="cell-id=be75126c-10e4-47d3-8929-921426e7bb10"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <h1 id="Conditional-Image-Generation-with-Classifier-Guidance">Conditional Image Generation with Classifier Guidance<a class="anchor-link" href="#Conditional-Image-Generation-with-Classifier-Guidance">¶</a></h1> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=3415e731-d39d-4ec9-abd0-41fe60eeb239"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p><strong>Introduction.</strong> In our <a href="https://www.peterholderrieth.com/blog/2023/Sampling-Images-with-Diffusion-Models/">previous tutorial</a>, we showed how we can build an image generation machine. While that is pretty cool, it is not quite useful yet. Generating <strong>some</strong> image is not interesting, usually we want to control our generation process. We want to say something like: "give me an image with a cat on it" and then get an image of a cat. In the next 2 tutorials, we are going to show you 2 techniques to achieve our goal: 1. Classifier guidance and 2. Classifier-free guidance. Today, we are going to focus on <a href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.05233v4.pdf">classifier guidance</a>.</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=d6efdf40-7207-4000-9ad8-01fc2faba9bb"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p><strong>Let's formalize our goal.</strong> In this case, we want to sample an image $x$ specified under a goal variable $y$. E.g. $x$ could be an image of a handwritten digit, and $y$ is a class, e.g. the digit the image represents. Formally, we want to sample from the distribution $p(x|y)$ (the conditional distribution of $x$ given $y$). For example, if we set $y=4$, we want to sample novel images of 4's.</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=b8452bda-7eb5-42ac-a826-2493455b911a"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p><strong>Why does our previous approach not work?</strong> It is important to understand that in principle we could very easily sample from $p(x|y)$ with our previous (unconditional) diffusion model approach. We simple train the model on data (i.e. images) $x$ whose label is $y$. However, that would have two disadvantages:</p> <ol> <li><strong>Many more models:</strong> We would need to have a model for every class label $y$. This makes the dataset significantly smaller per model and we would need train a lot of models. Even worse, if $y$ is arbitrary text, then it is virtually impossible to train a model for every instance of $y$.</li> <li><strong>No cross-context learning:</strong> intuitively, you would want to have a model that leverages its learnings across class labels $y$. That would allow you to use much more data - which is always a good bet in machine learning :)</li> </ol> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=d762a9e4-753e-42d7-b09c-308eaa371933"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p><strong>Classifier guidance.</strong> Let's consider the task of sampling from the distribution $p(x|y)$ with diffusion models. Again, we would convert the data distribution $p_{0}(x|y)=p(x|y)$ into a noised distribution $p_{1}(x|y)$ gradually over time via an SDE with $X_t\sim p_{t}(x|y)$ for all $0\leq t \leq 1$. As we <a href="https://www.peterholderrieth.com/blog/2023/Diffusion-Models-with-Stochastic-Differential-Equations-A-Introduction-with-Self-Contained-Mathematical-Proofs/">have learnt</a> in our previous tutorials, we need an approximation of the score function $\nabla_{x}\log p_t(x|y)$ to reverse the noising process and to sample from $p_{0}(x|y)=p(x|y)$. Let's use <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayes%27_theorem">Bayes' rule</a> to compute: $$ p_t(x|y) = \frac{p_t(y|x)p_t(x)}{p_t(y)}$$ And therefore, $$ \begin{align*} \log p_t(x|y) =& \log(p_t(y|x)) + \log(p_t(x)) - \log(p_t(y)) \end{align*} $$ Taking the gradient gives: $$ \begin{align*} \nabla_{x} \log p_t(x|y) =&\nabla_{x}\log(p_t(y|x)) + \nabla_{x}\log(p_t(x)) - \nabla_{x}\log(p_t(y)) \\ =&\nabla_{x}\log(p_t(y|x)) + \nabla_{x}\log(p_t(x)) \end{align*}$$ The above term is very significant. The second term is basically our unconditional score model $\nabla_{x}\log(p_t(x))$. In other words, this is what we have already trained beforehand! Therefore, we only need a way to compute the first term. Let's look at a bit closer. The term $p_t(y|x))$ is the probability of $y$ given $x$ at time $t$. This conditional probability is basically what we learn when we train a classifier of $y$ given $x$, i.e. of predicting the label $y$ given a noised data point $x$. In practice, we often end up using a more sharp distribution $p_{t}(y|x)^s$ for a factor $s\geq 0$. Therefore, we use: $$ \begin{align*} \nabla_{x} \log p_t(x|y) =&s\nabla_{x}\log(p_t(y|x)) + \nabla_{x}\log(p_t(x)) \end{align*}$$ for a parameter $s$ that tunes how strong the classifier gradient should be. Even if you do not understand the above derivation, this term is very intuitive: <strong>classifier guidance changed the score to not only point into regions of high probability $p_t(x)$ but pushes into regions where also $p_t(y|x)$ is high.</strong></p> <p>In sum, we simply need to do the following for conditional generation:</p> <p><strong>Training:</strong></p> <ol> <li>Train an unconditional score model $s_{\theta}(x_t,t)=\nabla_{x}\log(p_t(x))$ (see previous tutorial)</li> <li>Train a train a classifier $q_{\phi}(y|x,t)$ of $y$ given $x$ - where $\phi$ are the parameters of our neural network and $x$ is a sample from $p_{t}$.</li> </ol> <p><strong>Sampling:</strong> At every time step, compute</p> <ol> <li>Unconditional score $s_{\theta}(x_t,t)\approx \nabla_{x}\log(p_t(x))$</li> <li>Gradient of conditional probability $\nabla_{x}\log q_{\phi}(y|x,t) \approx \nabla_{x}\log p_t(y|x)$.</li> <li>Run a diffusion time step with $s_{\theta}(x_t,t) + s\nabla_{x}\log q_{\phi}(y|x,t)$.</li> </ol> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=4708a44f-7805-4486-b85d-908187de665b"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>The <strong>crucial insight here is that for conditional generation, we only need to train an additional classifier on our noisy data $p_{t}(x)$ and we are done - without every needing the re-train our unconditional diffusion model!</strong></p> </div> </div> </div> </div><div class="jp-Cell In order to do so, we use the pytorch automatic differentiation framework to compute $\nabla_{x}\log q_{\phi}(y|x)$. We do the following:</p> <ol> <li>Convert x into a tensor that has <code>requires_grad=True</code> to signal pytorch to compute gradients.</li> <li>Send both x and t to GPUs</li> <li>Pass them through the classifier. Note that the classifier compute $\log q_{\phi}(y|x)$ for every possible $y=0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7,9$.</li> <li>Therefore, we need to select the one that we want by selecting for the target $y_0=y$.</li> <li>Finally, we sum up: $$\sum\limits_{i=1}^{B}\log p_t(y_0|x_i)$$ where $B$ is the batch size.</li> <li>Finally, we take the gradient of the sum which gives us $\nabla_{x_i}q_{\phi}(y_0|x_i)$ for each element in the batch.</li> </ol> </div> </div> </div> </div><div class="jp-Cell jp-CodeCell jp-Notebook-cell jp-mod-noOutputs" id="cell-id=c3c0ba24-173f-4f52-97cd-227a8e543316"> <div We modified our <code>run_backwards</code> function to take two arguments:</p> <ol> <li><code>cond_grad_func</code>: a conditional gradient function, which is <code>get_classifier_gradient</code> here. This is $s\nabla_{x_t}q_{\phi}(y_0|x_t,t)$.</li> <li><code>target</code>: an integer $y_0$ giving the label that we want to condition on.</li> </ol> <p>We then run the diffusion backwards in the same way as before. The only lines of code that changes are:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre><span></span><span class="k">if</span> <span class="n">cond_grad_func</span> <span class="ow">is</span> <span class="ow">not</span> <span class="kc">None</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="n">cond_grad</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">cond_grad_func</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="n">to</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">device</span><span class="p">),</span> <span class="n">time_vec</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="n">to</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">device</span><span class="p">),</span> <span class="n">target</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="n">to</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">change</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="n">device</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="n">cond_grad</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="p">(</span><span class="n">step_size</span><span class="o">*</span><span class="n">ItoSDE</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="n">_mult_first_dim</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">g_squared</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="n">cond_grad</span><span class="p">))</span> <span class="n">change</span> <span class="o">+=</span> <span class="n">cond_grad</span>
