jp-MarkdownOutput " data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <h2 id="6.From-noise-to-signal:-Generative-modelling-with-SDEs">6.From noise to signal: Generative modelling with SDEs<a class="anchor-link" href="#6.From-noise-to-signal:-Generative-modelling-with-SDEs">¶</a></h2> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput " data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>So far, we have learnt that we have can construct stochastic differential equations evolving from time $t=0$ to a certain time $t=T$. For affine drift coefficients, we have learnt how compute their distributions over time. This is relevant for generative AI because, as we have learnt, SDEs converge under certain constraints to a normal distribution $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ <strong>regardless (!!!) of their initial distribution $X_0\sim p_0$</strong>! Let me explain why that is significant...</p> <p>Remember that for generative AI, the goal is to sample from a data distribution $p_{\text{data}}$, e.g. $p_{\text{data}}$ could be a distribution of images over celebrities and the goal is to generate a new picture of a fictional celebrity. If we set $p_{\text{data}}=p_0$ as the initial distribution of an SDE, we know that after a certain time $T>0$, the distribution of $X_T$ is $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ (up to some negligible error). <strong>The significance of this is that while we cannot draw novel samples from $p_{\text{data}}$ (beyond what we have in our train data), we can sample from $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ easily</strong>. Therefore, the idea is go backwards: if we run an SDE backwards in time (from $t=T$ to $t=0$), we could sample $X_T\sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)$ and then evolve the SDE backwards to reach $X_0\sim p_{\text{data}}$. In other words, we would have learnt to sample from our data distribution. Here is a figure from <a href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2011.13456.pdf">Song et al.</a> that illustrates this:</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput " data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p><img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="image.png"></p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput " data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>In this chapter, we are going to learn how to reverse an SDE in time enabling us to build generative AI models.</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput " data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <h3 id="6.1.-Time-reversal-formula">6.1. Time-reversal formula<a class="anchor-link" href="#6.1.-Time-reversal-formula">¶</a></h3> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput " data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>An important result of SDEs is that we can reverse them in time. What we mean with that is the following: imagine that we run an SDE $$dX(t) = f(X_t,t)dt+g(t)dW_t$$ from time $t=0$ ($X_0\sim p_0$) to time $X_{T}\sim p_{T}$. <strong>The question is: if we started only with a sample from $X_T\sim p_T$, is there an SDE that runs backwards in time (from $t=T$ to $t=0$) and gives the same stochastic process as $X_t$?</strong></p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput " data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>Let's first define what a reverse-time SDE is. It is given by the following equation:</p> $$d\bar{X}_t= \bar{f}(X_t,t)dt + \bar{g}(t)d\bar{W}_t $$<p>where the Brownian motion $\bar{W}_u$ runs backwards in time (i.e. $\bar{W}_{t-s}-\bar{W}_{t}$ is independent of $\bar{W}_t$ for $s>0$). In discretized terms, that means: $$\begin{align*} \bar{X}_{t-s}-\bar{X}_t &\approx - s\bar{f}(\bar{X}_t,t)+\sqrt{s}\bar{g}(t)\epsilon \quad \text{ where } \epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)\end{align*}$$</p> <p><strong>So we can reframe our question: given $f,g$, are there $\bar{f},\bar{g}$ such that the reverse-time diffusion process $\bar{X}_{t}$ has the same distribution as the forward-time process $X_t$?</strong></p> <p>An important result from the 80s from mathematician <a href="https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0304414982900515">Brian Anderson</a> is: Yes! <strong>We can reverse an SDE by setting</strong></p> $$\begin{align*}\bar{g}&=g\quad(\text{g-Reverse})\\ \bar{f}(x,t)&=f(x,t)-g^2(t)\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\log p_{t}(x)\quad(\text{f-Reverse})\end{align*}$$<p>where $p_t(x)$ is the density of the distribution of $X_t$. In other words, the reverse-time SDE is given by: $$d\bar{X}_t= [f(X_t,t)-g^2(t)\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\log p_{t}(\bar{X}_t)]dt + g(t)d\bar{W}_t \quad(\text{Reverse-SDE})$$</p> <p>Intuitively, the statement says: to reverse an SDE, we need to:</p> <ol> <li>Add Gaussian noise $\bar{W}_t$ with the same variance drift as the forward equation.</li> <li>Go $f(x,t)$ backwards (i.e. $-f(x,t)$) and account for the change in distribution $p_t(x)$.</li> </ol> <p><strong>Proof?:</strong> Later, I also give a self-contained derivation of the above time-reversal formula. As this is not relevant for the machine learning practitioner, I have put in the appendix at the end of this tutorial.</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput " data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <h3 id="6.2.-Score-based-generative-modelling-with-SDEs">6.2. Score-based generative modelling with SDEs<a class="anchor-link" href="#6.2.-Score-based-generative-modelling-with-SDEs">¶</a></h3><p>The time-reversal formula allows us to learn how to generate samples from a probability distribution $p_{\text{data}}$. In order to sample from $p_{\text{data}}$, we follow these steps:</p> <ol> <li><strong>Setup - select converging SDE.</strong> Select $f(x,t)$ and $g(t)$ with affine drift coefficients such that $X_t$ converges to a static distribution $q$ (e.g. $q=\mathcal{N}(0,1)$).</li> <li><strong>Training - learn scores:</strong> Train a deep neural network $s_{\theta}(x,t)$ to approximate $s_{\theta}(x,t)=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\log p_t(x)$ with $p_t$ is the distribution of $X_t$ when $X_0\sim p_{\text{data}}(x)$.</li> <li><strong>Deployment - run reverse-time SDE with trained score:</strong> To sample from $p_{\text{data}}$:\ 3.1. Sample $X_T\sim q$.\ 3.2. Run-reverse time SDE from $T$ to $0$ replacing $\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\log p_{t}$ with $s_{\theta}$: $$d\bar{X}_t= [f(X_t,t)-g^2(t)s_{\theta}(x,t)dt + g(t)d\bar{W}_t$$ <pre><code>  I.e. numerically with step size $s>0$:
</code></pre> $$\begin{align*} \bar{X}_{t-s} &\approx \bar{X}_t +s\left[g^2(t)s_{\theta}(\bar{X}_t,t)-f(\bar{X}_t,t)\right]+\sqrt{s}g(t)\epsilon \quad \text{ where } \epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)\quad(\text{Reverse Dynamics})\end{align*}$$</li> </ol> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput " data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p><strong>Score-based models?</strong>: the above explains why the methods are called <strong>score-based generative models</strong>: to generate the reverse-time SDE, we "only" need to train a model to predict the score $\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\log p_t(x)$ - everything else is defined by us.</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput " data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p><strong>Remark - annealed Langevin dynamics:</strong> Remember from the <a href="ASD">previous tutorial</a> that Langevin dynamics can sample from $p_{\text{data}}$ by the following (reverse-time) iteration: $$\bar{X}_{t-h} = \bar{X}_t+h\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\log p_{\text{data}}(\bar{X}_t)+\sqrt{h}\epsilon\quad \text{ where } \epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)\quad\text{(Langevin Dynamics)}$$</p> <p>For the variance exploding SDE, we have that:</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput " data-mime-type="text/markdown"> $$\begin{align*}\bar{X}_{t-s}\approx\bar{X}_t+h\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\log p_t(\bar{X}_t)+\sqrt{h}\epsilon \end{align*}$$<p>for $h=sg^2(t)$. So basically, the right-hand side is a simulation of Langevin dynamics with a slight difference: instead of using $p_{\text{data}}$ at every time step, we use a noisy version $$p_t(x_t)=\int \mathcal{N}(x_t;x_0,\beta(t))p_{\text{data}}(x_0)dx_0$$ As the noise $\beta(t)$ is decreasing to zero for $t\to 0$, $p_{t}\to p_{\text{data}}$ - i.e. we anneal the distribution to the data distribution. This gives the above method <strong>annealed Langevin dynamics</strong>. The advantage of annealed Langevin dynamics is in regions of low probability $p_{\text{data}}$, we have very poor estimates of the scores (just out of data scarcity). Therefore, upon initialization, one uses a noised version (introducing bias to remove high variance). <a href="https://yang-song.net/blog/2021/score/">Yang Song's blog</a> has great illustrations for that.</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput " data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <h3 id="6.3.-Training-scores">6.3. Training scores<a class="anchor-link" href="#6.3.-Training-scores">¶</a></h3> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput " data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>The question remains how we train the neural network $s_{\theta}$. Due to the construction, the shape of the input and output of $s_{\theta}$ are simply the shape of our data vectors $X_0\sim p_{\text{data}}$. Therefore, the architecture $s_{\theta}$ is likely going to depend on the data type we are looking at - for images, we might want to pick a transformer or a CNN.</p> <p>It remains to define a differentiable loss $L(\theta)$. A natural choice is to use the mean-squared error to the true score $\frac{\partial}{\partial x}p_t(x)$ weighted by a function $\lambda:[0,T]\to\mathbb{R}_{+}$: $$\begin{align*} L_{\text{untractable}}(\theta)=&\frac{1}{T}\int\limits_{t=0}^{T}\lambda(t)\mathbb{E}_{x_0\sim p_{\text{data}}}\mathbb{E}_{x_t\sim p_t(\cdot|x_0)}\left[\|s_{\theta}(x_t,t)-\frac{\partial}{\partial x_t}\log p_t(x_t)\|^2\right]dt\\ =&\mathbb{E}_{t\sim\text{Unif}_{[0,T]}}\left[\lambda(t)\mathbb{E}_{x_0\sim p_{\text{data}}}\mathbb{E}_{x_t\sim p_t(\cdot|x_0)}\left[\|s_{\theta}(x_t,t)-\frac{\partial}{\partial x_t}\log p_t(x_t)\|^2\right]\right]\\ \end{align*} $$ where have replaced the integral with a Monte Carlo estimate of the integral. Notice that in the above, we cannot compute $p_t(x_t)$ as it depends on $p_0=p_{\text{data}}$ - which we are trying learn! However, it holds that for $X_t|X_0\sim p_{t|0}(\cdot|X_0)$:</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput " data-mime-type="text/markdown"> $$\begin{align*} p_t(x_t)=\mathbb{E}_{x_0\sim p_{\text{data}}}\left[p_{t|0}(x_t|x_0)\right]=\int p_{t|0}(x_t|x_0)p_{\text{data}}(x)dx \end{align*} $$<p>and therefore $$\begin{align*} \frac{\partial}{\partial x_t}\log p_t(x_t) =&p_{t}(x_t)^{-1}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_t}p_t(x_t)\\ =&p_{t}(x_t)^{-1}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_t}\int p_{t|0}(x_t|x)p_{\text{data}}(x)dx\\ =&p_{t}(x_t)^{-1}\int \frac{\frac{\partial}{\partial x_t}p_{t|0}(x_t|x)}{p_{t|0}(x_t|x)}p_{\text{data}}(x)p_{t|0}(x_t|x)dx\\ =&p_{t}(x_t)^{-1}\int \frac{\partial}{\partial x_t}\log p_{t|0}(x_t|x)p_{\text{data}}(x)p_{t|0}(x_t|x)dx\\ =&\int \frac{\partial}{\partial x_t}\log p_{t|0}(x_t|x)p_{0|t}(x|x_t)dx\\ =&\mathbb{E}_{x_0'\sim p_{0|t}(\cdot|x_t)}\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial x_t}\log p_{t|0}(x_t|x_0')\right] \end{align*} $$</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput " data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>and therefore $$\begin{align*} \|s_{\theta}(x_t,t)-\frac{\partial}{\partial x_t}\log p_t(x_t)\|^2=&\|\mathbb{E}_{x_0'\sim p(\cdot|x_t)}\left[s_{\theta}(x_t,t)-\frac{\partial}{\partial x_t}\log p_{t|0}(x_t|x_0')\right]\|^2\\ \leq &\mathbb{E}_{x_0'\sim p(\cdot|x_t)}\left[\|s_{\theta}(x_t,t)-\frac{\partial}{\partial x_t}\log p_{t|0}(x_t|x_0')\|^2\right]\\ \end{align*} $$ and inserting that equation in $L_{\text{untractable}}$ we get: $$\begin{align*} L_{\text{untractable}}(\theta) =&\mathbb{E}_{t\sim\text{Unif}_{[0,T]}}\left[\lambda(t)\mathbb{E}_{x_0\sim p_{\text{data}}}\mathbb{E}_{x_t\sim p_t(\cdot|x_0)}\left[\|s_{\theta}(x_t,t)-\frac{\partial}{\partial x_t}\log p_t(x_t)\|^2\right]\right]\\ \leq &\mathbb{E}_{t\sim\text{Unif}_{[0,T]}}\left[\lambda(t)\mathbb{E}_{x_0\sim p_{\text{data}}}\mathbb{E}_{x_t\sim p_t(\cdot|x_0)}\left[\mathbb{E}_{x_0'\sim p(\cdot|x_t)}\left[\|s_{\theta}(x_t,t)-\frac{\partial}{\partial x_t}\log p_{t|0}(x_t|x_0')\|^2\right]\\\right]\right]\\ = &\mathbb{E}_{t\sim\text{Unif}_{[0,T]}}\left[\lambda(t)\mathbb{E}_{x_0\sim p_{\text{data}}}\mathbb{E}_{x_t\sim p_t(\cdot|x_0)}\left[\|s_{\theta}(x_t,t)-\frac{\partial}{\partial x_t}\log p_{t|0}(x_t|x_0)\|^2\right]\\\right]\\ = & L_{\text{simple}}(\theta) \end{align*} $$ where have used that if $x_0'\sim p_{0|t}(\cdot|x_t)$ and $x_t\sim p_{t}$, then also $x_0'\sim p_0=p_{\text{data}}$. <strong>Note, we can compute $L_{\text{simple}}(\theta)$ because it only depends on the conditional distribution $p_{t|0}(x_t|x_0)$ which is normally distributed because we assumed affine drift coefficients:</strong> $$p_{t|0}(x_t|x_0)=\mathcal{N}(x_t;\mathbb{E}[X_t|X_0=x_0];\mathbb{V}[X_t|X_0=x_0])$$</p> <p>As we have shown above, for affine drift coefficients we can simply compute $\mathbb{E}[X_t|X_0=x_0],\mathbb{V}[X_t|X_0=x_0]$ in closed form. The score is then given by:</p> $$\begin{align*} \frac{\partial}{\partial x_t}\log p_{t|0}(x_t|x_0)=-\frac{x_t-\mathbb{E}[X_t|X_0=x_0]}{\mathbb{V}[X_t|X_0=x_0]} \end{align*} $$<h3 id="6.4-Score-networks-as-denoising-machines">6.4 Score networks as denoising machines<a class="anchor-link" href="#6.4-Score-networks-as-denoising-machines">¶</a></h3><p>Using that $p_{t|0}$ is Gaussian, we can set $X_t|X_0\sim \sqrt{\mathbb{V}[X_t|X_0=x_0]}\epsilon+\mathbb{E}[X_t|X_0]$ where $\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbb{1}_d)$ and therefore: $$ \begin{align*} L_{\text{simple}}(\theta) &=\mathbb{E}_{t\sim\text{Unif}_{[0,T]}}\left[\lambda(t)\mathbb{E}_{x_0\sim p_{\text{data}}}\mathbb{E}_{x_t\sim p_t(\cdot|x_0)}\left[\|s_{\theta}(x_t,t)+\frac{x_t-\mathbb{E}[X_t|X_0=x_0]}{\mathbb{V}[X_t|X_0=x_0]}\|^2\right]\\\right]\\ &=\mathbb{E}_{t\sim\text{Unif}_{[0,T]}}\left[\lambda(t)\mathbb{E}_{x_0\sim p_{\text{data}}}\mathbb{E}_{\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbb{1})}\left[\|s_{\theta}(\sqrt{\mathbb{V}[X_t|X_0=x_0]}\epsilon+\mathbb{E}[X_t|X_0],t)+\frac{\epsilon}{\sqrt{\mathbb{V}[X_t|X_0=x_0]}}\|^2\right]\\\right]\\ &=\mathbb{E}_{t\sim\text{Unif}_{[0,T]}}\left[\lambda(t)\mathbb{E}_{x_0\sim p_{\text{data}}}\frac{1}{\mathbb{V}[X_t|X_0=x_0]}\mathbb{E}_{\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbb{1})}\left[\|\epsilon_{\theta}(\sqrt{\mathbb{V}[X_t|X_0=x_0]}\epsilon+\mathbb{E}[X_t|X_0],t)-\epsilon\|^2\right]\\\right] \end{align*} $$ for an alternative <strong>denoising network</strong> $$ \begin{align*}&\epsilon_{\theta}(x_t,t)=-s_{\theta}(x_t,t)\sqrt{\mathbb{V}[X_t|X_0=x_0]}\\ \Leftrightarrow &s_{\theta}(x_t,t)=-\frac{\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)}{\sqrt{\mathbb{V}[X_t|X_0=x_0]}}\end{align*}$$</p> <p>The network $\epsilon_{\theta}$ is called a denoising network because it learns to predict the noise that has converted the original image $x_0$ to the distorted image $x_t=\sqrt{\mathbb{V}[X_t|X_0=x_0]}\epsilon+\mathbb{E}[X_t|X_0]$. Therefore, <font color="red"> <strong>training a diffusion model is equivalent to training a neural network to predict the noise that distorted your input.</strong></p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput " data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <h2 id="7.-Summary">7. Summary<a class="anchor-link" href="#7.-Summary">¶</a></h2> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput " data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>Finally, we summarize the key takeaways from this tutorial:</p> <ol> <li><strong>Ito-SDEs.</strong> Ito-SDEs are defined by a deterministic drift $f$ and a random drift $g$ and a Brownian motion $W_t$: $$dX(t) = f(X_t,t)dt+g(t)dW_t$$</li> <li><strong>Simulation.</strong> One can simulate SDEs in discrete time by the Euler-Maryuama method: $$X_{t+s} = X_{t} + sf(X_{t},t)+g(t)\sqrt{s}\epsilon\quad, \epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{1}_d)$$</li> <li><strong>Affine drifts allow simple formulas.</strong> All SDEs relevant for machine learning have affine drift coefficients, i.e. $f(x,t)=a(t)x+b(t)$, one can derive closed-form expressions for conditional expectations and conditional variance and the distributions are normal (i.e. the process is Gaussian).</li> <li><strong>Training.</strong> Training a diffusion model corresponds to training a neural network $s_{\theta}(x,t)$ to optimize the score $s_{\theta}(x,t)\approx p_t(x)$ by minimizing the following loss: $$\begin{align*} L(\theta) = &\mathbb{E}_{t\sim\text{Unif}_{[0,T]}}\left[\lambda(t)\mathbb{E}_{x_0\sim p_{\text{data}}}\mathbb{E}_{x_t\sim p_t(\cdot|x_0)}\left[\|s_{\theta}(x_t,t)-\frac{\partial}{\partial x_t}\log p_{t|0}(x_t|x_0)\|^2\right]\\\right]\\ \end{align*}$$</li> <li><strong>Sampling.</strong> Sampling from a diffusion model corresponds to sampling an inital value $\bar{X}_T\sim q$ from a distribution $q$ that the SDE converges to. Subsequently, the SDE is evolved in reverse-time with approximate score $s_{\theta}$ given by: $$\begin{align*}&d\bar{X}_t= [f(X_t,t)-g^2(t)s_{\theta}(x,t)dt + g(t)d\bar{W}_t\\ \Leftrightarrow& \bar{X}_{t-s} \approx \bar{X}_t +s\left[g^2(t)s_{\theta}(\bar{X}_t,t)-f(\bar{X}_t,t)\right]+\sqrt{s}g(t)\epsilon \quad \text{ where } \epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)\end{align*}$$</li> <li><strong>Most important SDEs for diffusion models:</strong> There are 2 big types of SDEs used in the literature for diffusion models:\ <pre><code>A. The variance-preserving (VP) SDE exponentially converges to $\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{1}_d)$. The discrete counterpart is the first diffusion model introduced by [Sohl-Dickstein et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1503.03585.pdf).\
B. The variance-exploding (VE) SDE has a constant expectation value $\mathbb{E}[X_0]=\mathbb{E}[X_t]$ and a rescaled version converges to $\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{1}_d)$. The discrete counterpart is[ Score matching with Langevin dynamics (SMLD)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.05600).</code></pre> </li> </ol> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput " data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p><strong>What's next?</strong> In my <a href="INSERT">next tutorial</a>, we are going to put the theory we developed into practice and train a diffusion model to generate novel images. We are also going to learn abouut conditional generation of images based on text as well as learn about Neural ODEs and their connection to diffusion models.</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput " data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <h2 id="Appendix:-A-Mathematical-Derivation-of-the-time-reversal-formula">Appendix: A Mathematical Derivation of the time-reversal formula<a class="anchor-link" href="#Appendix:-A-Mathematical-Derivation-of-the-time-reversal-formula">¶</a></h2> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput " data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>In the following, I would like to present a simple derivation of the time-reversal formula. <strong>For the reader only interested in using the formula above, I recommend to skip this section.</strong> Most proofs (including the <a href="https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0304414982900515">original one</a>) rely on <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolmogorov_forward_equations">Kolmogorov's forward equation</a>. However, I don't like using a complicated formula to develop intuition for another formula. Therefore, I developed the below derivation that does not rely on methods outside of traditional probability theory.</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput " data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>The approach of the proof is to express $g,f$ in terms of the following limits: \begin{align*}f(x,t) = \lim\limits_{h\to 0}\frac{\mathbb{E}[X_{t+h}-X_{t}|X_t=x]}{h}\\ g^2(t) = \lim\limits_{h\to 0}\frac{\mathbb{V}[X_{t+h}|X_t=x]}{h} \end{align*} This a reverse definition: instead defining $X_{t}$ via $f,g$ as above, we can also define $f,g$ implicitly via the above equations deriving from $X_t$. We use this identity to derive the equation for $\bar{f},\bar{g}$ from $\bar{X}_t$.</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput " data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <h3 id="A.1.-Deriving-$%5Cbar%7Bf%7D$">A.1. Deriving $\bar{f}$<a class="anchor-link" href="#A.1.-Deriving-$%5Cbar%7Bf%7D$">¶</a></h3> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput " data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>Since $\bar{f}$ is the time-reversal of the SDE, we can compute: \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[\bar{X}_{t}-\bar{X}_{t+h}|\bar{X}_{t+h}=x] &=\int (x_t-x)p_{t|t+h}(x_t|x)dx_{t} \\ &=\int (x_t-x)p_{t+h|t}(x|x_{t})p_t(x_t)/p_{t+h}(x)dx_t\\ &\approx\frac{1}{p_{t+h}(x)}\int (x_t-x)\mathcal{N}(x;x_t+hf(x_{t},t),hg(t)))p_t(x_t)dx_t \end{align*} We can approximate $f(x_t,t)$ via a Taylor approximation: \begin{align*} f(x_{t},t) = f(x,t)+(x_t-x)\frac{\partial}{\partial x}f(x,t) \end{align*} and do a substution $x_t\to x_t-hf(x,t)$ and get: \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}[\bar{X}_{t}-\bar{X}_{t+h}|\bar{X}_{t+h}=x] \approx&\frac{1}{p_{t+h}(x)}\int (x_t-x)\mathcal{N}(x_t+hf(x,t)+h(x_t-x)\frac{\partial}{\partial x}f(x_t,t);x,hg(t)))p_t(x_t)dx_t\\ =&\frac{1}{p_{t+h}(x)}\int (x_t-x)\mathcal{N}(x_t+h(x_t-hf(x,t)-x)\frac{\partial}{\partial x}f(x,t);x,hg(t)))p_t(x_t)dx_t\\ &-\frac{hf(x,t)}{p_{t+h}(x)}\int\mathcal{N}(x_t+h(x_t-hf(x,t)-x)\frac{\partial}{\partial x}f(x,t);x,hg(t)))p_t(x_t)dx_t\\ =&A+B \end{align*} Using partial integration, we get that: \begin{align*} \frac{A}{h} &= \frac{hg^2(t)}{hp_{t+h}(x)(1+h\frac{\partial}{\partial x}f(x,t))} \int (1+h\frac{\partial}{\partial x}f(x,t))\frac{x_t+h(x_t-hf(x,t)-x)\frac{\partial}{\partial x}f(x,t)-x}{hg^2(t)}\mathcal{N}(x_t+h(x_t-hf(x,t)-x)\frac{\partial}{\partial x}f(x,t);x,hg^2(t)))p_t(x_t)dx_t \\&-\frac{hg^2(t)}{hp_{t+h}(x)(1+h\frac{\partial}{\partial x}f(x,t))} \int (1+h\frac{\partial}{\partial x}f(x,t))\frac{h(x_t-hf(x,t)-x)\frac{\partial}{\partial x}f(x,t)}{hg^2(t)}\mathcal{N}(x_t+h(x_t-hf(x,t)-x)\frac{\partial}{\partial x}f(x,t);x,hg^2(t)))p_t(x_t)dx_t\\ =&-\frac{g^2(t)}{p_{t+h}(x)(1+h\frac{\partial}{\partial x}f(x,t))}\int \frac{\partial}{\partial x_t}\mathcal{N}(x_t+h(x_t-hf(x,t)-x)\frac{\partial}{\partial x}f(x,t);x,hg^2(t)))p_t(x_t)dx_t\\\ &-\frac{1}{p_{t+h}(x)} \int (x_t-hf(x,t)-x)\frac{\partial}{\partial x}f(x,t)\mathcal{N}(x_t+h(x_t-hf(x,t)-x)\frac{\partial}{\partial x}f(x,t);x,hg^2(t)))p_t(x_t)dx_t\\ =&\frac{g^2(t)}{p_{t+h}(x)(1+h\frac{\partial}{\partial x}f(x,t))}\int \mathcal{N}(x_t+h(x_t-hf(x,t)-x)\frac{\partial}{\partial x}f(x,t);x,hg^2(t)))\frac{\partial}{\partial x_t}p_t(x_t)dx_t\\ &-\frac{1}{p_{t+h}(x)} \int (x_t-hf(x,t)-x)\frac{\partial}{\partial x}f(x,t))\mathcal{N}(x_t+h(x_t-hf(x,t)-x)\frac{\partial}{\partial x}f(x,t);x,hg^2(t)))p_t(x_t)dx_t\\ \to&\frac{g^2(t)}{p_{t}(x)(1+0)}\int \delta_{x}\frac{\partial}{\partial x_t}p_t(x_t)dx_t\\ &-\frac{1}{p_{t}(x)} \int (x_t-x)\frac{\partial}{\partial x}f(x,t))\delta_{x}p_t(x_t)dx_t\\ =&\frac{g^2(t)}{p_{t}(x)}\frac{\partial}{\partial x}p_t(x)-0=g^2(t)\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\log p_t(x) \end{align*} where $\delta_{x}$ is the dirac delta distribution and we have used that for $x_n\to x$ and $\mu^2_n\to 0$ also for any regular function $G$:</p> $$ \begin{align*} \int \mathcal{N}(z;x_n,\mu^2_n) G(z)dz \to \int\delta_{x} p_t(z)dz = G(x)\quad\text{as }n\to\infty \end{align*} $$ </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput " data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>For $B$, we compute: \begin{align*} \frac{B}{h} =& -\frac{f(x,t)}{p_{t+h}(x)}\int\mathcal{N}(x_t+h(x_t-hf(x,t)-x)\frac{\partial}{\partial x}f(x,t);x,hg(t)))p_t(x_t)dx_t\\ &\to-\frac{f(x,t)}{p_t(x)}p_t(x)=-f(x,t) \end{align*}</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput " data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>As a result, we get that: \begin{align*} \bar{f}(x,t) = -\lim_{t\to 0}\frac{1}{h}\mathbb{E}[\bar{X}_{t-h}-\bar{X}_{t}]=-\lim_{t\to 0}\frac{B+A}{h}=f(x,t)-g^2(t)\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\log p_t(x) \end{align*}</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput " data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <h3 id="A.2.-Deriving-$%5Cbar%7Bg%7D$-for-Gaussian-SDEs">A.2. Deriving $\bar{g}$ for Gaussian SDEs<a class="anchor-link" href="#A.2.-Deriving-$%5Cbar%7Bg%7D$-for-Gaussian-SDEs">¶</a></h3> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput " data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>Next, we derive $\bar{g}$. In the following, we assume that the Ito-SDE describes a <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_process">Gaussian process</a>, i.e. the distribution of tuple $(X_{t_1},X_{t_2},\dots,X_{t_n})$ is Gaussian. As we have shown above, this is in particular the case for affine drift coefficients $f$ - so basically this proof includes all SDEs relevant for machine learning.</p> <p>For now, let's assume that the initial distribution of $X_0$ is deterministic, i.e. $X_0=x_0$. Let's write down the distribution of $X_{t-h},X_{t}$ for all $t,h\geq 0$:</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput " data-mime-type="text/markdown"> $$X_{t-h}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbb{E}[X_{t-h}|X_0],\mathbb{V}[X_{t-h}|X_0])$$$$X_{t}|X_{t-h}=x_{t-h}\sim\mathcal{N}(x_{t-h}+hf(x_{t-h},t-h),hg^2(t-h))$$<p>Therefore, we know that the $\text{Cov}[X_{t-h},X_{t}]$ looks as follows: $$ \begin{align*} \text{Cov}[X_{t-h},X_{t}] &= \begin{pmatrix} \mathbb{V}[X_{t-h}|X_0] & \mathbb{V}[X_{t-h}|X_0] \\ \mathbb{V}[X_{t-h}|X_0] & \mathbb{V}[X_{t-h}|X_0] +hg^2(t-h) \end{pmatrix}\\ \mathbb{E}[[X_{t-h},X_{t}]^T|X_0] &= [\mathbb{E}[X_{t-h}|X_0],\mathbb{E}[X_{t-h}|X_0]+hf(X_{t-h},t-h)]^T \end{align*} $$</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput " data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>We use the formula of <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multivariate_normal_distribution#:~:text=Conditional%20distributions">conditional multivariate Gaussians</a> to get: $$\begin{align*} \bar{g}^2(t)=\lim\limits_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}\mathbb{V}[\bar{X}_{t-h}|\bar{X}_t,X_0]=&\lim\limits_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}\left[\mathbb{V}[\bar{X}_{t-h}|X_0]-\frac{\mathbb{V}[\bar{X}_{t-h}|X_0]^2}{\mathbb{V}[X_{t-h}|X_0] +hg^2(t-h)}\right]\\ =&\lim\limits_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}\mathbb{V}[\bar{X}_{t-h}|X_0]\left[1-[1+\frac{hg^2(t-h)}{\mathbb{V}[\bar{X}_{t-h}|X_0]}]^{-1}\right]\\ =&\mathbb{V}[\bar{X}_{t}|X_0]\frac{d}{dh}\left[1-[1+\frac{hg^2(t-h)}{\mathbb{V}[\bar{X}_{t-h}|X_0]}]^{-1}\right]_{|h=0}\\ \end{align*}$$</p> <p>We compute the derivative: $$\begin{align*} &\frac{d}{dh}_{| h=0}\left[[1+\frac{hg^2(t-h)}{\mathbb{V}[X_{t-h}|X_0]}]^{-1}-1\right]\\ =&\left[-[1+\frac{hg^2(t-h)}{\mathbb{V}[X_{t-h}|X_0]}]^{-2}\right]_{|h=0}\frac{d}{dh}_{| h=0}\frac{hg^2(t-h)}{\mathbb{V}[X_{t-h}|X_0]}\\ =&-\frac{d}{dh}_{| h=0}\frac{hg^2(t-h)}{\mathbb{V}[X_{t-h}|X_0]}\\ =&-\frac{\mathbb{V}[X_{t-h}|X_0][g^2(t-h)-h2g(t-h)g'(t-h)]-hg^2(t-h)\frac{d}{dh}\mathbb{V}[X_{t-h}|X_0]}{(\mathbb{V}[X_{t-h}|X_0])^2}_{|h=0}\\ =&-\frac{g^2(t)}{\mathbb{V}[X_{t}|X_0]} \end{align*}$$ And therefore, $$\begin{align*} \bar{g}^2(t)=g^2(t) \end{align*} $$</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput " data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>For non-deterministic initial distribution $X_0\sim p_0$, we use the rule of <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_of_total_variance">law of total variance</a> to get as well: $$\begin{align*} \frac{1}{h}\mathbb{V}[\bar{X}_{t-h}|\bar{X}_t]&=\frac{1}{h}[\mathbb{E}_{X_0}[\mathbb{V}[\bar{X}_{t-h}|\bar{X}_t,X_0]]+\mathbb{V}[\mathbb{E}_{X_0}[X_{t-h}|X_t,X_0]]\\ &=\frac{1}{h}\mathbb{E}_{X_0}[\mathbb{V}[\bar{X}_{t-h}|\bar{X}_t,X_0]]+\frac{1}{h}\mathbb{V}[-h\bar{f}(X_t,t)]\\ &=\frac{1}{h}\mathbb{E}_{X_0}[\mathbb{V}[\bar{X}_{t-h}|\bar{X}_t,X_0]]+h\mathbb{V}[\bar{f}(X_t,t)]\\ &\to g^2(t)+0 \end{align*}$$</p> <p>This finishes the proof.</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput " data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p><strong>Note:</strong> stricly speaking, we would still need to show that the reverse-time process is actually an SDE at all. However, in the Gaussian case, it is trivial to show that the reverse-time Gaussian process is also a Gaussian process. Due to the above derivation, it is then also an SDE.</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> </body> </html>

excitement in recent years as powerful generative models that allow to generate novel images from text prompts (see <a href="https://stablediffusionweb.com/">Stable Diffusion</a>), <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.01776">molecules</a>, or <a href="https://www.bakerlab.org/2023/07/11/diffusion-model-for-protein-design/">proteins</a>. Diffusion models rely on <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stochastic_differential_equation">Stochastic Differential Equations</a>, a hard to digest mathematical concept for somehow new to the field. Therefore, I want to provide a bit more intuition to SDEs. In this tutorial, we will study a specific stochastic differential equation: the <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langevin_equation">Langevin diffusion</a> - a fundamental SDE to understand diffusion models. In the <a href="">next tutorial</a>, we will then dive deeper into Ito-SDEs - the basis for most concepts.</p> <p><strong>Introduction to Langevin diffusion.</strong> The Langevin diffusion has been discovered in physics to describe the motion of particles driven by random and deterministic forces. Due to the random forces, it is a <strong>stochastic process</strong> that in generative AI describes the evolution of a probability distribution over time. It is named after the French mathematician <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Langevin">Paul Langevin</a>, who first introduced the concept in the early 20th century.</p> <p>In the context of generative modeling, the Langevin diffusion is often used as a way to sample from a probability distribution $p(\mathbf{x})$ that is difficult to sample from directly. $p$ can be the distribution of random portraits of people - and we can generate a novel image from it. The following are examples of images generated by a Langevin diffusion from <a href="https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2019/file/3001ef257407d5a371a96dcd947c7d93-Paper.pdf">Song and Ermon 2019</a> trained on the MNIST dataset (left), the CelebA dataset (middle), and CIFAR-10 (right):</p> <p><img alt="image-3.png" src="data:image/png;base64,"/></p> <p>The idea of the Langevin diffusion is to start with an initial "seed" sample $X_{0}$ and then iteratively update it (i.e. compute $X_{t+s}$ from $X_t$) using a stochastic differential equation that pushes $X_t$ into regions of high probability $p$. If we run the updates long enough ($t\to\infty$), we have</p> <p>$$\mathbb{P}(X_t\in A) \approx p(A)$$</p> <p>In other words, by evolving $X_t$ over time long enough, we can approximately generate samples from a probability distribution $p$. If $p$ describes a distribution over images or text, we can generate novel images, text, and many more data types. Here is an example from <a href="https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/improving-diffusion-models-as-an-alternative-to-gans-part-2/">Nvidia</a> describes the evolution of an initial white noise seed $X_0$ to a sample $X_t$ that gives a realistic sample of a cat: <img alt="image-7.png" src="data:image/png;base64,"/></p> <p><strong>What is this post about?</strong> The goal of this post is to give a hands-on introduction to the Langevin diffusion - understand why it is working and how it can be used. We are focusing here on explaining the mathematical concept to help you understand the literature on diffusion models.</p> <p><strong>What's next?</strong> In my <a href="ASD">next tutorial</a>, I will you a thorough introduction into the world SDEs and how they can be used for diffusion models.</p> </div> </div> </div> </div><div class="jp-Cell jp-CodeCell jp-Notebook-cell jp-mod-noOutputs" Preparation: Define tools to visualize and construct distributions<a class="anchor-link" href="#1.-Preparation:-Define-tools-to-visualize-and-construct-distributions">¶</a></h2> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=d75d82b3"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>Let's begin by first constructing a probability distribution $p(\mathbf{x})$ that we would like to sample from. In this post, we consider <strong>2-dimensional</strong> Gaussian mixture distributions. A Gaussian mixture is given by a weighted sum of Gaussian distributions: $$p(\mathbf{x}) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{n}q_j \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x};\mu_i,\Sigma_{i}), \quad \text{where } q_j\in\mathbb{R},\sum\limits_{j=1}^{n}q_j = 1,\mu_i\in\mathbb{R}^2,\Sigma_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times 2}$$</p> <p>This chapter describes how we construct such distributions. <strong>For the rushed reader, this chapter can safely skipped.</strong></p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=a9ba223d"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <h3 id="1.1.-Visualize-probability-densities">1.1. class="p">]</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kc">None</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">mixture_probs</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="n">np</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="n">array</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kc">None</span><span class="p">):</span>
<span class="w"> </span><span class="sd">"""Function to compute Gaussian mixtures.</span> <span class="sd"> representation - str: how to represent the Gaussian mixture. </span> <span class="sd"> Can be either "density" or "score"</span> <span class="sd"> x - np.array: shape (n,k) - data, i.e. n locations in k-dimensional euclidean space.</span> <span class="sd"> mean_list - list of mean arrays of shape (k): means of individual Gaussian distributions</span> <span class="sd"> cov_list - list of covariance matrices of shape (k,k): covariance matrices of individual Gaussian distributions</span> <span class="sd"> """</span>
<span class="k">if</span> <span class="n">cov_list</span> <span class="ow">is</span> <span class="kc">None</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="n">cov_list</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nb">len</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">mean_list</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="o">*</span><span class="p">[</span><span class="kc">None</span><span class="p">]</span>
<span class="k">if</span> <span class="n">mixture_probs</span> <span class="ow">is</span> <span class="kc">None</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="n">mixture_probs</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">np</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="n">ones</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="nb">len</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">mean_list</span><span class="p">))</span><span class="o">/</span><span class="nb">len</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">mean_list</span><span class="p">)</span>
<span class="k">if</span> <span class="n">representation</span> <span class="o">==</span> <span class="s2">"density"</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="c1">#1. The density of a Gaussian mixture is the weighted sum of its individual</span> <span class="c1">#Gaussian distributions.</span> <span class="n">density</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">np</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="n">zeros</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">shape</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="nb">len</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">))</span> <span class="k">for</span> <span class="n">mean</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="n">cov</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="n">prob</span> <span class="ow">in</span> <span class="nb">zip</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">mean_list</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="n">cov_list</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="n">mixture_probs</span><span class="p">):</span> <span class="n">density</span> <span class="o">+=</span> <span class="n">prob</span><span class="o">*</span><span class="n">gaussian_density</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="n">mean</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="n">mean</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="n">cov</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="n">cov</span><span class="p">)</span>
<span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">density</span>
<span class="k">elif</span> <span class="n">representation</span> <span class="o">==</span> <span class="s2">"score"</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="c1">#2. The score of a Gaussian mixture is given by the weighted sum of the individual</span> <span class="c1">#gradients of the probability density divided by the density.</span>
<span class="c1">#Initalize:</span> <span class="n">score</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">np</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="n">zeros</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">shape</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="nb">len</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">),</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="o">.</span><span class="n">shape</span><span class="p">[</span><span class="mi">1</span><span class="p">]))</span>
<span class="c1">#Nominator is the mixture of the gradient of the density:</span> <span class="k">for</span> <span class="n">mean</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="n">cov</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="n">prob</span> <span class="ow">in</span> <span class="nb">zip</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">mean_list</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="n">cov_list</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="n">mixture_probs</span><span class="p">):</span> <span class="n">score</span> <span class="o">+=</span> <span class="n">prob</span><span class="o">*</span><span class="n">get_gaussian</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">representation</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="s2">"gradient_of_density"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="n">mean</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="n">mean</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="n">cov</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="n">cov</span><span class="p">)</span>
<span class="c1">#Denominator of the score is the density:</span> <span class="n">density</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">get_gaussian_mixture</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="s2">"density"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="n">mean_list</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="n">cov_list</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="n">mixture_probs</span><span class="p">)</span>
<span class="c1">#Compute fraction:</span> <span class="n">score</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">score</span><span class="o">/</span><span class="n">density</span><span class="p">[:,</span><span class="kc">None</span><span class="p">]</span> <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">score</span>

id="2.-The-Langevin-Stochastic-Differential-Equation">2. The Langevin Stochastic Differential Equation<a class="anchor-link" href="#2.-The-Langevin-Stochastic-Differential-Equation">¶</a></h2> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=b4b08610"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>The Langevin Diffusion describes a <strong>Stochastic Differential Equation</strong>, i.e. the evolution of random variable $X_t\in\mathbb{R}$ over time $t\geq 0$:</p> <p>\begin{align*} dX_t = \nabla\log p(X_t) + \sqrt{2}W_t \end{align*} where $W_t$ is a Brownian motion. <strong>If you are not familar with SDEs, you are probably wondering at this point what such a notation means or even what a Brownian motion is.</strong> For our purposes, the above equation simply means that the above process can be approximately computed by the following discretization: \begin{align*} X_{t+s} = X_{t}+s\nabla\log p(X_{t})+\sqrt{2s}\epsilon \end{align*} where $s>0$ is the step size and $\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}_d)$. In other words, the update of the step $X_t$ is performed by:</p> <ol> <li>Going into the direction of the gradient: $\nabla\log p(X_{t})$.</li> <li>Adding some random Gaussian noise $\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)$.</li> </ol> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=4633526e"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <h3 id="2.1.-Intuitively-understanding-the-Langevin-SDE">2.1. Intuitively understanding the Langevin SDE<a class="anchor-link" href="#2.1.-Intuitively-understanding-the-Langevin-SDE">¶</a></h3> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=6d0fc8a2"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>Intuitively understand the Langevin Diffusion is simpler than you might think. Remember that our goal is to sample from $p(\mathbf{x})$. That means that $X_t$ evolves over time such that $\mathbb{P}(X_t\in A)\approx p(A)$. The direction of the gradient $\nabla\log p(X_{t})$ pushes $X_t$ into directions of high probability, i.e. where $p(\mathbf{x})$ is high. That ensures that we move to regions of high probability. Let's plot the score $\nabla\log p(X_{t})$ and look at it.</p> </div> </div> </div> </div><div class="jp-Cell jp-CodeCell jp-Notebook-cell jp-mod-noOutputs" id="cell-id=d2e5eb88"> <div tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>As one can see above, the score vector field $\nabla\log p(X_{t})$ points into directions of high probability. If we just moved into the direction of $\nabla\log p(X_{t})$, we would simply perform <strong>gradient ascent</strong> (the sister algorithm of the famous <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gradient_descent">gradient descent</a> algorithm). In particular, we would very quickly end up in a local maximum of $p(\mathbf{x})$ - there would be no movement anywhere, we would be stuck.</p> <p>Therefore, we need to inject some noise into our diffusion $X_t$ to keep some randomness in the process. With the Gaussian noise injected, the Langevin diffusion moves into directions of high probability $p(\mathbf{x})$ <strong>on average.</strong> That makes it plausible that this allows us to sample from $p(\mathbf{x})$.</p> <p><font color="blue"><font size="4"> <strong>Intuitively, the Langevin diffusion is gradient ascent maximing the log-probability $\log p(\mathbf{x})$ injected with random Gaussian noise $\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)$.</strong></font></font></p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=4974c07e"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <h3 id="2.2.--A-Mathematical-Derivation-of-the-Langevin-Diffusion">2.2. A Mathematical Derivation of the Langevin Diffusion<a class="anchor-link" href="#2.2.--A-Mathematical-Derivation-of-the-Langevin-Diffusion">¶</a></h3> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=67d15951"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>Let's try to understand mathematically why the Langevin Diffusion converges to the probability distribution $p(\mathbf{x})$ over time. Our goal is to show that $p$ is an equilibrium distribution for the Langevin diffusion for $\tau\to 0$. I.e. if $X_t\sim p$, then also $X_{t+s}\sim p$ for every $s>0$.</p> <p>Let $f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ be a test function, i.e. a smooth (infinitely differentiable) function with compact support. Then it suffices to show that $\mu_{t}(f)=\mathbb{E}[f(X_{t})]$ is constant across time $t$ for $\tau\to 0$ (assuming regularity of $p$, in particular $p>0$ everywhere).</p> <p>Let's do a Taylor approximation of order 2: \begin{align*} \mu_{t+\tau}(f)=& \mathbb{E}[f(X_{t+\tau})]\\ =&\mathbb{E}[f(X_{t}+\tau\nabla\log p(X_{t})+\sqrt{2\tau}\epsilon)]\\ \approx&\mathbb{E}[f(X_t)]+\mathbb{E}[\nabla f(X_t)^T(\tau\nabla\log p(X_{t})+\sqrt{2\tau}\epsilon))]\\ &+ \frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}[(\tau\nabla\log p(X_{t})+\sqrt{2\tau}\epsilon)^T\nabla^2 f(X_t)(\tau\nabla\log p(X_{t})+\sqrt{2\tau}\epsilon)]\\ =&\mathbb{E}[f(X_t)]+\tau\mathbb{E}[\nabla f(X_t)^T(\nabla\log p(X_{t})]+\sqrt{2\tau}\mathbb{E}[\nabla f(X_t)^T\epsilon]\\ &+\frac{\tau^2}{2}\mathbb{E}[\nabla\log p(X_{t})^T\nabla^2 f(X_t)\nabla\log p(X_{t})]\\ &+\sqrt{2\tau}\mathbb{E}[\epsilon^T\nabla^2 f(X_t)(\tau\nabla\log p(X_{t}))]\\ &+\tau\mathbb{E}[\epsilon^T\nabla^2 f(X_t)\epsilon]\\ =&\mu_t(f)+A+B+C+D+E \end{align*} Let's compute the summands $A,B,C,D,E$ step by step. We know that $B,D=0$ as $\mathbb{E}[\epsilon]=0$ and $\epsilon$ is independent of $X_t$. Let's compute A by partial integration and show that it equals $-E$: \begin{align*} A=&\tau\mathbb{E}[\nabla f(X_t)^T\nabla\log p(X_{t})] \\ =&\tau \int \nabla f(x)^T\nabla\log p(x)p(x)dx \\ =&\tau \int \nabla f(x)^T\nabla p(x)dx \\ =&-\tau \int \text{tr}(\nabla^2 f(x))p(x)dx \\ =&-\tau\mathbb{E}[\text{tr}(\nabla^2 f(X_t))]\\ =&-\tau\mathbb{E}[\epsilon^T\text{tr}(\nabla^2 f(X_t))\epsilon]\\ =&-E \end{align*} where have used $X_t\sim p$ by assumption. Therefore, we can see that $\mu_{t+\tau}(f)-\mu_{t}(f)=A+C+E=-E+C+E=C$ and hence, \begin{align*} \frac{|\mu_{t+\tau}(f)-\mu_t(f)|}{\tau} \approx & \frac{|C|}{\tau}\\ \leq & \frac{\tau^2}{2\tau}\mathbb{E}[|\nabla\log p(X_{t})^T\nabla^2 f(X_t)\nabla\log p(X_{t})|]\\ \leq & \frac{\tau}{2}\|g\|_{\max}\ \end{align*} where we use that $g(x)=\nabla\log p(x)^T\nabla^2 f(x)\nabla\log p(x)$ is bounded because it is a continuous function with compact support. Therefore, it holds that \begin{align*} \frac{d}{dt}\mu_t(f)=0 \end{align*} In other words, we have that for all $t,s>0$: $$\mathbb{E}[f(X_{t})]=\mu_t(f)=\mu_{t+s}(f)=\mathbb{E}[f(X_{t+s})]$$</p> <p>By approximating the indicator function $\mathbb{1}_{A}$ for a rectangle $A=[a_1,b_1]\times\dots\times[a_d,b_d]\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ with smooth functions $f_k$, we an derive that:</p> <p>$$\mathbb{P}(X_t\in A) = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{1}_A(X_{t})] = \lim\limits_{k\to\infty} \mathbb{E}[f_k(X_{t})] = \lim\limits_{k\to\infty} \mathbb{E}[f_k(X_{t+s})] = \mathbb{P}(X_{t+s}\in A) $$</p> <p>In other words, the distribution of $X_t$ is constant over time</p> <p><strong>Remark:</strong> While it is not a sufficient condition strictly speaking that a distribution $p$ is an equilibrium distribution of an SDE for $X_t$ to converge to $p$, it is sufficient in many cases. The goal is this post is to give mathematical intuition for the Langevin diffusion. For a rigorous proof, we refer to the <a href="https://projecteuclid.org/journals/annals-of-probability/volume-47/issue-4/Couplings-and-quantitative-contraction-rates-for-Langevin-dynamics/10.1214/18-AOP1299.full">mathematical literature</a>.</p> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=1f97e0f4"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <h2 id="4.-Implement-Langevin-Diffusion">4. Implement Langevin Diffusion<a class="anchor-link" href="#4.-Implement-Langevin-Diffusion">¶</a></h2> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>Finally, let's implement the Langevin diffusion: \begin{align*} X_{t+s} = X_{t}+s\nabla\log p(X_{t})+\sqrt{2s}\epsilon \end{align*}</p> </div> </div> </div> </div><div class="jp-Cell jp-CodeCell jp-Notebook-cell jp-mod-noOutputs" Conclusion<a class="anchor-link" href="#6.-Conclusion">¶</a></h2> </div> </div> </div> </div> <div class="jp-Cell jp-MarkdownCell jp-Notebook-cell" id="cell-id=a50085e3-0509-438b-a67a-cf192cf2918a"> <div class="jp-Cell-inputWrapper" tabindex="0"> <div class="jp-Collapser jp-InputCollapser jp-Cell-inputCollapser"> </div> <div class="jp-InputArea jp-Cell-inputArea"><div class="jp-InputPrompt jp-InputArea-prompt"> </div><div class="jp-RenderedHTMLCommon jp-RenderedMarkdown jp-MarkdownOutput" data-mime-type="text/markdown"> <p>We are done! The Langevin diffusion is a fundamental concept for sampling from a probability distribution and hence for generative AI.
